Mr Ron Sao : This report is the annual report of the Public Accounts Committee from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. During the year, the committee considered 23 Auditor General reports and followed up on nine of them. Our findings are in our report titled Review of Selected Auditor General Reports 2022–2024. The committee tabled three reports during this time. Following the lead of previous committees, we also held a state budget briefing for all members. Committee members and staff attended the Australasian Council of Public Accounts Committees conference in Hobart. It was a chance to meet our counterparts from across the region, including the Pacific islands, and understand a bit more of the work of each jurisdiction and learn from their experience.

The committee also began an inquiry into whether a government land rent scheme or similar scheme would be feasible for Western Australians. The standing orders allow the committee to inquire into any matter connected with the receipt and expenditure of public moneys. Given that government land is a public asset, the inquiry is considering whether leasing government land at an appropriate rent, with suitable financing, could support home ownership at a reasonable cost to the state. Land is a significant part of the cost of a home. Leasing government land rather than selling it could lower the cost of entry, and the land would stay in public ownership for future public use. The inquiry is focused on moderate and middle-income households that may not be able to enter the private housing market. It does not cover social or community housing.

I thank my fellow committee members for their cooperation and contribution throughout the year, including the Deputy Chair, the member for Central Wheatbelt; and the member for Bassendean, the member for Cottesloe and the member for Swan Hills. I would also like to thank the committee staff for their professionalism and support during the period and in preparing this report. I also want to thank everyone who has attended our briefings, given evidence at hearings or made submissions. Their help on the inquiry and the scrutiny of public expenditure has been appreciated.
Before I close, I want to acknowledge the Auditor General and wish her the very best as she recovers from her health issues. I commend the report to the house.

Ms Sandra Brewer (Cottesloe) (10:13 am) : I want to commend the work of the Public Accounts Committee and draw attention to the important parts of the annual report for the period 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. I am really pleased to be part of this committee, whose role is to examine the expenditure of public money, supporting accountability across state government entities and local governments. Members will know that is a strong commitment and a motivating reason for me being in this place. Of the three reports tabled during the period, it was the Review of Selected Auditor General Reports 2022–2024, tabled on 18 June 2026, that I found to be critical. This report summarised the outcomes of our consideration of 23 Auditor General reports and the follow-up of nine reports tabled in the period.

I want to draw attention to report 14, Administration of the Perth Parking Levy. This report exposed the dire lack of progress to implement the recommendations of the Auditor General's inquiry into the administration of the Perth parking levy. The levy is collected from central Perth property owners to fund urban development and transport initiatives in the Perth CBD. In the recent state budget, it held an estimated actual balance of $194 million as at 30 June 2026. The Auditor General made scathing findings in February 2023. The report found that there was no plan for how money in the account should be used. Money was approved for use on non-transport projects and five projects with unspecified priority. The department's administration is not fully transparent. Consultation with the City of Perth is inconsistent and inadequately assessed, evaluated and publicly reported.

It was up to our committee, the Public Accounts Committee, to do a review, three years later, after that critical Auditor General report. We found that no improvements had been made. The Minister for Transport and Major Infrastructure should have implemented the five clear recommendations to improve transparency, accountability and controls, yet, over three years later, the Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure has made no progress. The department is yet to prepare the regulations under the Perth Parking Management Act 2024 or a revised Perth parking policy. These instruments are required before the 2024 act can come into force, but the department makes the excuse that it is currently preparing them.

The department has also made excuses that phase 2 of the Perth Greater CBD Transport Plan can only be reconsidered when the 2024 act is proclaimed. Phase 2 of the Perth Greater CBD Transport Plan is critical to the contributors to the levy fund, as it has the potential to unlock investment, reduce congestion and increase visitation and tourism. By not progressing the plan, the government is failing to support Perth CBD stakeholders to realise a vision for Perth to be a vibrant, thriving city centre. Correspondence provided to the Public Accounts Committee by the Director General of DTMI made it clear that the levy continues to be used as a ministerial fund. Rather than preparing policies and plans with key stakeholders, he revealed that DTMI submits budget proposals for consideration by the minister and that projects are at the minister's discretion. The submission by the director general shows little action has been taken and there has been little progress to date, and demonstrates a lack of regard for delivering value for taxpayer funds. Without the important work of our Public Accounts Committee, matters such as this would not be revealed.

I commend my parliamentary colleagues, principal research officers Kim Payne and Suzanne Veletta, and Elise Milroy, Jacob Keillor and Darren Seet. I would also like to reiterate the comments from the member for Central Wheatbelt wishing the Auditor General good health in her recovery.

heading: Public housing
subject: Public housing
parts: (a) notes that at 31 August 2026 there were 23,958 public housing applications in Western Australia;

(b) notes the findings of the Auditor General in Management of Housing Maintenance Information , 6 August 2025, including that only 51% of vacant property work orders met the department's 14-day completion target and that the state lacks a clear end-to-end measure of how long homes sit empty between tenants;

(c) notes that parliamentary answers recorded 29 vacant public housing properties in the City of Busselton as at 28 February 2026, and that similar vacancy figures for Bunbury and other regions are not routinely published in a form the public can use;

The government's other line, from the same minister last October, was that the vast majority of properties were returned in 14 days. That is typical of the government. It focuses on the easy jobs, celebrating meeting the basic expectations, but avoiding talking about where it is failing. The minister's own figure was a 22-week average. The representing minister will maybe tell us that it is complicated, and there are complications amongst that.

Let me quote someone who actually looked at the department's record. On 6 August last year, the Auditor General tabled a report called Management of Housing Maintenance Information. The Auditor General found that the department spent $241 million between 2019 and 2025 maintaining houses while they were empty. Nearly one dollar in five of the entire maintenance budget went into houses with nobody living in them. The Auditor General found that the time taken just to issue a first works order on an empty house had gone from nine days to 14 days. That is quite a bit of difference there—two weeks before anyone even orders the works. The Auditor General also found that only 51% of work orders on empty houses met the department's own 14-day target. What was the department's answer to missing its own target? It told the Auditor General that the 14-day target was no longer achievable. The plan is not to hit the target; the plan is to move the target. Then there is a line that probably should worry every person on the waitlist, and I will read it out exactly as it is written on page 25 of the report. It states:
Housing and Works does not have targets for completing all work on vacant property and how long it should take from one tenant leaving to another moving in.
No target, no deadline and no accountability. The one measure the department keeps count of is the days per work order. The Auditor General says that the measure:
… does not represent the underlying goal of getting tenants into homes as quickly as possible.

Those are the Auditor General's words. The department told her it would fix that as it moved into new maintenance contracts from July 2026. Has it, though? On 15 September, the department's own website said the new contracts will start in July 2028. The government has approved extending the old contracts. It has approved pushing out the audited contracts to 2028. That is two more years of the same contractors and 22,000 work orders a month, yet, still, nobody is measuring how long a house sits empty.

Western Australia already spends more public money on public housing than any other state. It is $23,428 a year in recurrent costs for every dwelling, which is nearly double that of New South Wales. That is a good thing; we are spending a lot of money on housing, but of all the states, we have the most expensive system and the slowest turnaround. The problem does not seem to be underfunding; the problem may well be mismanagement.
The Auditor General wrote this:
… I urge Housing and Works to do more with the data it already has to improve efficiency now for the benefit of taxpayers and people waiting for a home.

This motion asks for four things, and not one of those is asking for new builds. The first thing is a monthly public housing vacancy register by local government area—occupied, vacant, coming back and ready to allocate. For every empty house, we need the reason it is empty and the date it is scheduled to come back. The department already uses those categories. It calls them returning and non-returning voids. We should just publish them.

The second thing is that the only number that matters for empty stock is the days from the last tenant out to the next tenant in. We need the median and average by region, not just days per work order. We need the actual days until a person is able to move in. That should be written into maintenance contracts as a key performance indicator now. Let us not wait until the extension the government has given—not until July 2028. Do it now. The department has already told the Auditor General that it intends to be more transparent, so why not do it now? Do not make people wait two more years for it.

The third thing is a time-limited public housing restoration taskforce. It should report to Parliament every quarter and then be wound up. It should not be another working group that reports back in two years, but a real taskforce that finishes its task in a targeted manner.

heading: Public housing
subject: Public housing
parts: Hon Rob Horstman (10:40 am) : I also rise to support the motion moved by Hon Rod Caddies, which raises a very important issue facing communities across the whole of Western Australia. Housing is not simply a social policy issue in regional WA; it is an economic issue, a workforce issue and is increasingly becoming an education issue. Hon Neil Thomson has already mentioned Kalgoorlie–Boulder, and I will carry on that theme, as housing supply is a particularly concerning issue in that part of the state. It is an example of how a growing regional economy is impacted when housing supply fails. While government properties in the region sit vacant, families are struggling to find homes, essential workers are competing for accommodation and, to a certain degree, most concerningly in terms of the future we are trying to build in the region, university students are unable to secure somewhere to live. The fundamental question that this motion puts forward is, to me, very straightforward: Why do public homes remain empty when the need for housing is so great and so enormous? This motion is about transparency, accountability and making better use of homes funded by taxpayers' money.

I have some quick comments around the scale of the public housing problem we face. The number of applications for WA public housing as at 31 August 2026, as referenced, was pushing 24,000, and only 51% of vacant property work orders meet the target. From a Kalgoorlie perspective, as of June 2026, there were 107 vacant public homes. The Auditor General's findings in an August 2025 report identified that just over half the vacant property work orders met the 14-day target imposed and that the state lacks a clear end-to-end measure of how long homes remain empty between tenancies. Through answers to parliamentary questions, it was revealed that 107 properties were vacant as of June 2026. It is not just Kalgoorlie where there are vacant homes; Laverton and Leonora are in the same position. I am not suggesting every one of those houses is immediately habitable; some will require substantial repairs and some will require refurbishment. It is precisely why we need to know what condition they are in, what work needs to be done and when they can be returned to use. A vacant property without a clear plan for its future is an unacceptable outcome when we face a housing crisis.

In August, I raised some concerns about the accommodation crisis at the Western Australian School of Mines in Kalgoorlie. A report from Curtin Student Guild and Making Rent Fair WA describes that students are couch surfing, sleeping in vehicles and even living in tents because they are unable to secure accommodation. The figures reported are actually quite extraordinary. There are approximately 800 students in the current cohort of WASM students and only 266 accommodation beds available. There is a numerical gap of 534 beds relative to that cohort. I am not at all suggesting that every person attending WASM needs accommodation to be provided for them. However, it does raise a question about the limited capacity of the purpose-built accommodation for that institution compared with the size of the student cohort. International and postgraduate students are identified as particularly affected. We are talking about students studying at one of Australia's most important and prestigious education institutions when it comes to the resources sector. These are the future mining engineers, geologists and technical professionals who will help sustain an industry that underpins Western Australia's economy and effectively bankrolls the Cook Labor government's spending agenda. How can we expect students to come to Kalgoorlie, complete their qualifications and potentially build careers, raise families and stay in the Goldfields when they cannot find a safe and affordable place to live? We cannot keep talking about the mining skills shortage while overlooking the accommodation needed when we train the next generation. The Cook Labor government needs to work with Curtin University, industry and the community to deliver additional student accommodation. We need clear funding commitments and clear construction timeframes.

Hon Philip Scott (11:05 pm) : I rise to support the motion moved by my colleague Hon Rod Caddies. I want to say at the outset that it asks for nothing that a competent landlord would not already know: Which houses are empty? Why and when will they be back in use? My colleague has given the house the count. I want to spend my 10 minutes on two things he did not have time for: where the maintenance money goes and the people who are waiting. Last November, the government was asked about the head maintenance contract for public housing. The answer given in this place on 20 November was that the contract with Programmed Facility Management was until 30 June 2026 and it was $158.5 million in the 12 months to 30 September 2025. That is $158 million a year to one head contractor. The Auditor General tells us on page 25 of her report that:
Housing and Works audits 5.7% of work orders and recoups around $1 million in overpayments annually.

Of that 5.7%, between 24% and 30% were noncompliant and 27% were not in line with the agreed schedule of rates. Only 1.62% of audits were physical inspections. That is somebody actually going out to the house. From a sample of one work order in 17, the department found $4.8 million in overpayments between 2019 and 2024. The government was asked what it would find if it audited half of them. The answer received was that it does not form part of the report. No—it is the part that should form the next report. When a tenant falls behind on the rent, the department follows it up straight away. When a contractor bills for work on an empty house, the bill is checked one time in 17, and an empty house is the easiest house to bill for. There is no tenant to say whether the work was done. Those contracts were due to run out on 30 June this year—they did not. On 15 September, the department's website said it had the government's approval to seek an extension of the existing head maintenance contracts to 30 June 2028 and that the new contract would not start until July 2028. The department told the Auditor General that the new contracts would carry new categories for empty houses and new performance measures. That fix is now two years further away, and in the meantime, the same contractors keep the same work under a system that checks one bill in 17. Whether the one measure that matters, which is the number of days from one tenant leaving to the next moving in, goes into the extended contracts with a target and published, is exactly the question this motion puts.

Now I turn to the people. A renter knows what an empty house means. The landlord has other priorities. When the landlord is the state and 23,809 applicants are waiting, that is a policy choice, whether or not anyone in government admits to making it.

heading: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
subject: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
parts: It gives me great pleasure to speak more broadly to the activities of the Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations and its 96th report titled 2025–26 Activity Report. Although it is not a departure from the practices of other committees, the estimates committee is somewhat unique in that it opens up its processes to the participation of other members in this chamber in a way that is not often the case for our rather established standing committees. It is useful for the chamber to consider the breadth of issues and subjects that the committee considered over the 2025–26 period of time that were outside of the standard budgetary set-piece processes—namely, the budget estimates process, which most, if not all, members of this chamber are familiar with, and the annual report hearings process, which is, on occasion, a more select and possibly a more bespoke process. If I am to reflect upon my role in chairing those two different processes, I probably have a preference for the annual report hearing, if only because we have a document that is better comprehended and more contemporaneous on behalf of the witnesses who are present. We normally have a smaller gathering of interested members, but those participating members who turn up probably have a deeper interest in the operations of the particular agency being examined. That does not reflect upon the performance or conduct of members during budget estimates, but budget estimates is a more unwieldy beast, to which respective chairs over time have endeavoured their best to bring a measure of order. It has also been my observation, my practice, that the chair through that budget estimates period is likely to receive some pretty contemporaneous, sometimes emotive, feedback on the conduct of those hearings and the conduct of the chair. I have become inured to some of this. My skin is thick, but I have endeavoured, if I might humbly say, to have taken upon myself the feedback that is presented to me and to use that feedback in the most productive way I can possibly muster in the circumstances, but I digress somewhat.

Going back to the report, it includes an element that I can lead into on another occasion, perhaps, to talk about the forthcoming annual report season, but I will not take advantage of that today. Instead, I want to reflect upon section 4 of this report that speaks to the committee's conference participation, in particular, that of myself, Hon Dan Caddy and our advisory officer, Carmen Cummings, who had to suffer the indignity of travelling to Hobart in April. I say "indignity", and I do not intend the full meaning of that word, but it was a difficult travail. We attended the Australasian Council of Public Accounts Committees or ACPAC, which took place on 20 and 21 April in Hobart. It was very well hosted by the Tasmanian parliamentary Public Accounts Committee. We were accompanied by our counterpart committee—indeed, the full Public Accounts Committee from the Legislative Assembly. I note the active participation of the chair of that committee, the member for Cannington, who was an able participant. That was an interesting meeting because it brought together counterpart committees like the Public Accounts Committee across the majority of Australian jurisdictions and their Auditors General. In the course of the presentations and the interaction around the margins of these kinds of events, you come away with some insights into what constitutes a productive relationship, a constructive and professional but arms-length relationship, between these parliamentary committees that have estimates-like functions and the statutory responsibilities of Auditors General in other Australian jurisdictions. For what it is worth, I think we in Western Australia get that balance right.

As well as looking at the financial operations of the government, which is within the terms of reference of the Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations, it is also an explicit term of reference that the committee consult with the Auditor General. I understand as well that that is a term of reference also explicitly outlined for the Public Accounts Committee in the Legislative Assembly. That consultation can take many forms, but largely speaking we undertake that consultation through as regular a dialogue with the Office of the Auditor General as frequently as we can. There will always be opportunities for performance enhancement and constructive dialogue, but I think in Western Australia we probably get the balance right. I will reflect very briefly on other Australian jurisdictions. I think it would be exceedingly difficult, for example, irrespective of the government of the day, to undertake the duties and functions of the Tasmanian Auditor-General by virtue of the fact that they are operating in a very small population and dealing with issues of great public contention. I also reflect on the performance and function of the Auditor-General in Darwin, who operates under constraints that I was not familiar with, which in my mind, with the greatest of respect to counterparts in that jurisdiction, probably undermine the independence of the function. I think we should take some stock of the importance of the independence of the Office of the Auditor General as we have it in WA.

That said, a variety of presentations and reflections were given by counterpart Auditors General, but there was a reference made to a document that was published in, I believe, November last year. It is called the Independence of the Australasian Auditors General Report 2025. I will just cite very briefly where Western Australia sat. I think this is out of 10 or 12 jurisdictions. It provided a ranking of WA's overall independence as third, the bronze medal position across Australasia. It was at least a podium finish. The ranking, however, slipped to sixth overall in 2025. As I was reflecting, each office has its own jurisdictional context. The matter that seemed to be reflected on, which potentially drove down WA's ranking, was the amendments made under the Auditor General Amendment Act 2022, some of the provisions of which I understand are still unproclaimed. Sometimes, however, these things need to be taken into proper context. The other drivers seemed to be the rapid improvement in the overall independence of other jurisdictions, I think Victoria and New South Wales in particular.

In the time that I have available at this moment, I just note that we should always remain vigilant about the importance of these sorts of offices and to ensure that, to the best of our ability, they remain absolutely independent in order to provide that function of scrutiny and oversight that executive government needs. They are an aid to the community and to the Parliament and they need to be protected.

heading: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
subject: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
parts: The executive summary raised some points about that process. It talked about variation and the flexibility with which ministers and parliamentary secretaries of the Council represent the portfolios of ministers belonging to the Legislative Assembly. I think we also saw this in the broader estimates process, in that the current machinery-of-government changes that have led to what is described as an intricacy of current portfolio arrangements is real. I think members in this place feel that when they appear at estimates and in the annual report hearings, occasionally there is a fairly obtuse chain of command that we have to work through. The committee is certainly looking at how best to arrange that the people that members think they are going to be interrogating actually appear before us. We are aware of that. It is an issue, but I think with some skilful chairing and the hardworking ministers, parliamentary secretaries and staff, we are getting a reasonable outcome from that.

The consultation with the Auditor General is also a very important part of this committee's work. We met with the Auditor General and staff on 17 September. There were two parts to that hearing. The first part was a public hearing to discuss local government audit fees and there was a closed hearing subsequent to that. I want to focus a little bit of time on the issue of local government audit fees. This goes back to the passage of the Local Government Amendment (Auditing) Act 2017. Prior to that, it was up to the local government to hire an auditor for auditing arrangements, and the auditing process was done. Subsequent to that date, the Office of the Auditor General took over that role.

I want to reflect on some of the outcomes of that. I think back to when I was a shire councillor and these arrangements were being explained to us. I asked what the government expected the benefits of this change of process to be. A hardworking member of the Auditor General's staff was there, explaining what we could expect to see: better governance, more transparency and the better skilled auditing process somehow making the Shire of Wickepin a better council. I was a little cynical at the time, and I inquired whether the Auditor General's office actually audited government departments. I was informed that, of course, that is one of its key roles. I said, "The Department of Communities would be one of those audited." "Yes, absolutely, it is. That's one of ours." I said, "You've been keeping an eye on the Department of Communities over the years. That is good." This was at the time of the Paul Whyte saga. I am sure that members will remember the Paul Whyte saga and the extraordinary lack of governance in a department that was being audited by the Auditor General. I was being facetious, clearly. Those sorts of things happen, unfortunately. They happen rarely, but they do happen. They happen in mega-departments like the Department of Communities. Very occasionally, they happen in small local governments. The point I was trying to make was that I was not sure that we were going to get the result the government intended. We will see. Although this has been in place for some time now, I am not sure that the government has come back and said that the standard of local government governance was this and, through the audit process, it has been raised. I am not sure that it has done that.

Then, of course, there is the cost of the process. This was not free. Previous to 2017, there was a fee and a cost involved, but the costs skyrocketed when the Office of the Auditor General took over. At the City of Stirling, the City of Wanneroo or the City of Joondalup, an extra $20,000, $30,000 or $40,000 for an audit process is a rounding error. They are massive organisations. At the Shire of Wickepin, the Shire of Trayning or the Shire of Wandering, an extra 30 or 40 grand is a very significant increase in their costs. It needs a reasonable percentage rise in their rates just to cover that increase, and that happened immediately. We asked the Auditor General about that, and it was described to us as a series of jump-ups over the last couple of years to get back to something close to cost recovery. subject: Road Traffic Amendment (Disqualification Notices) Bill 2026
parts: The government already knows where the greatest risks lie. The challenge is turning that evidence into targeted action that prevents deaths and serious injury. We are not short on tools: we have the Western Australia Police Force, whose visible presence on our roads remains one of the most effective deterrents that we have; we have the Road Safety Commission; we have road treatments and place design that we know works; we have organisations such as RAC WA delivering programs like "bstreetsmart" to young Western Australians before they ever get behind the wheel; and we have the Road Trauma Trust Account funded primarily by camera infringement revenue, which exists to fund education campaigns, research and data collection, enforcement, infrastructure and post-crash support.

The Road Trauma Trust Account must be managed transparently with clear investment priorities and measurable outcomes. In October 2023, the Auditor General reported on its administration and identified shortcomings in expenditure priorities, in how funding applications were assessed and in how project outcomes were evaluated. Those are not minor findings. If we cannot measure whether the money is saving lives, we cannot know whether we are spending it in the right places.

heading: Local Government Amendment and Repeal Bill 2026
subject: Local Government Amendment and Repeal Bill 2026
parts: We are also introducing significant changes to address sustainability and foster local solutions. Let me be up front and clear: forced amalgamations are not on the government's agenda. However, amalgamation should not be seen as a dirty word or something that cannot be discussed. Western Australia has 139 local governments and 1,111 elected local council members. Those numbers are not sustainable. We must be willing to look at how to best enable local government to be structured, not just for today but for the decades to come. Key to this is the ability for local governments to have conversations with their neighbours to consider economies of scale that would benefit the community moving forward. We want to bring down the barriers that are preventing a voluntary sector-driven approach to bring local governments together. This will be achieved through the removal of what is known as the Dadour poll provision. Representatives across the sector have told the Cook government that the Dadour poll provision is an inhibitor to enduring structural reform. Removing this provision will give local governments greater flexibility to pursue local solutions. This does not change the minimum six-week consultation period and public inquiry process the Local Government Advisory Board carries out during an inquiry into a major boundary change. That will continue. The views of communities will continue to be considered in boundary change and amalgamation proposals. We will amend the criteria by which boundary changes and amalgamations are assessed by the Local Government Advisory Board to make the paramount considerations of the board, one, the long-term financial viability of local governments and, two, the effective delivery of local government services. Other considerations, such as communities of interest, demographics and history, are important and will still be considered.

Importantly, legislative change will not deliver joined-up local governments by itself. It needs to be supported by effective leaders in the local government sector who are willing to have honest conversations about what will best serve communities in the decades ahead. We are making other changes to modernise local government. For example, we will repeal the Local Government (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1960. This legislation is outdated. We will instead provide modern powers for local governments to deal with straying livestock. Regulations will deal with any residual matters. We will also protect people's privacy by regulating the public disclosure of the personal information of electors, ratepayers, candidates, council members and employees; modernise how fees and charges are set by allowing them to be amended during the year under delegation to the local government administration, rather than requiring a council decision; smooth the budget adoption process by allowing earlier advertising of proposed differential rates and, where a mistake is made in rates adoption, the ability to quash the rate and adopt a new one without going to the State Administrative Tribunal; and remove the need to appoint an independent deputy member to the independent presiding member of an audit, risk and improvement committee. These reforms respond to concerns raised by local governments and the Office of the Auditor General.

Our bill aims to create a modern, effective and sustainable local government sector for the years and decades to come for the benefit of every community in Western Australia. I commend the bill to the house.

Hon Kate Doust MLC does not support this recommendation for the reason that an oversighting mechanism is already in place in the form of the Legislative Council's Standing Orders that apply to the Legislative Council Public Administration and Finance Committee, which currently provide for that committee to consult regularly with the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administrative Investigations, the Auditor General, the Public Sector Standards Commissioner, the Information Commissioner, and (relevantly) "… any person holding an office of a like character."

In 2004, more than 20 years ago, the very question now before us was considered by those honourable members. Admittedly, there was a difference of opinion, and there is nothing wrong with that; that is entirely healthy. But I think there was clearly agreement by the members that, one, there should be a commissioner and, two, there should be a committee that oversees that commissioner. Should that be a dedicated specialist joint committee? The majority said yes, and that is what has happened over the last 20 years. Should it be handled by, shall we say, a more generalist committee of the Legislative Council, which was another option? Clearly that has not been the case up until now. Before members decide where they sit on this issue, it would be worthwhile for perhaps the Standing Committee on Procedure and Privileges to consider the 2004 report. Before we tear down the existing regime, it would be good to understand why the regime was put there in the first place.

heading: Joint Standing Committee on the Oversight of Certain Independent Office Holders
subject: Joint Standing Committee on the Oversight of Certain Independent Office Holders
parts: Of course, just by itself, the complexity of having that number of independent office holders overseen by one committee does not mean that we will reject this proposal, but, again, I think that the Standing Committee on Public Administration is already overseeing those statutory office holders, and I like to think that we are doing that fairly well. A broader remit requires resourcing and hearing time to match. Without them, individual officers risk receiving less attention. This has also been reiterated. We need to know how resourced this committee will be and how often it will hold hearings. Will specific guidelines be put in place to ensure that there is a requirement that office holders are met with at particular points in time? How frequently will the committee meet with office holders? What time will be available to the committee to make special inquiries alongside its annual reporting? Realistically, can we expect a committee of that size to be able to look at issues in a bit more detail? Members have already mentioned the vital responsibility of the Commissioner for Children and Young People and that that role should be overseen by a standalone committee. Now we are effectively saying that, despite this important recommendation, the Commissioner for Children and Young People is now going to be lobbed in with four or five other statutory office holders. That is a huge portfolio and there is a recommendation that it should stand alone; now it will just become one of five overseen by this bigger committee.

There is also a question about why these particular office holders were chosen. We include five, but we leave out the Public Sector Commissioner and the Auditor General. Why were some chosen and some not? Why are some included and some not? Again, there is not a lot of clarity in that space at all.

From my conversation with members, as has been reiterated, much of the push for this change stems from a lack of parliamentary oversight of our elections. There was a need to look at elections and have consistent oversight of the efficacies and issues during an election. Of course we agree on that. Earlier on, I and other parties actually wrote and signed a letter to that effect to say that there has to be a committee that looks at elections and there has to be independent oversight of the Electoral Commissioner, but how did that concern become a proposal for a super committee overseeing all these different offices? No-one can actually tell me. How did it morph into this massive committee that now overlaps with public admin? I think that is something we have to look at and consider. If the gap that prompted electoral oversight was the main issue, let us address that gap directly. Let us not look at all these other areas, creating all these other committees with all these other complexities.

parts: In terms of how that clawback works, foreign persons applying for the exemption must complete an application form and provide supporting documentation. If the taxpayer does not comply with the exemption requirements within the required period, foreign transfer duty will be assessed on the transaction and the taxpayer must notify the commissioner within two months at the end of the required period if they do not or will not meet the exemption requirements. If they fail to notify the commissioner, a penalty tax may be imposed under the Tax Administration Act 2003 and a fine of $20,000 may apply if the person is convicted of an offence for failing to notify. At the end of the required period, RevenueWA will verify the information provided in the exemption application, including whether the taxpayer has constructed the dwellings or subdivided the land, as part of its regular compliance activities. If it is determined that the taxpayer has provided false or misleading information in their application form, a penalty tax may be imposed under the Taxation Administration Act and prosecution action may be taken. heading: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
subject: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
parts: Hon Dr Steve Thomas : Yes, in this particular issue as well. Obviously, we are still working on and trying to deliver an outcome that provides some degree of certainty. What else can we glean from the second reading speech from the parliamentary secretary, which I am sure very high level staff put together? A couple of issues are key. It is important to be very clear here. The construction trust scheme in the bill applies exclusively to state government projects. It does not extend trustee obligations into the private sector or to lower tier subcontractors, which is a regulatory and administrative burden that has proven difficult in Queensland. Applying this level, or almost any level, of government regulation and legislation to the private sector in terms of security of payments in a system defined by contract law is fraught with danger. It is incredibly difficult for a government to insert itself into a legal argument at that kind of level in the private sector. I suspect that is why the Queensland Government has many critics of that. The bill before the house deals exclusively with government projects. I understand that the intent is to make sure that, on government-funded and government managed and controlled projects, subcontractors are being paid in an appropriate manner. I understand that. Like I say, this is the second or third version of this we have attempted in the 10 years that I have been in this particular chamber.

I can understand the argument that perhaps greater protection should be provided to the private sector. Again, if I had a simple solution that did not interfere with the legal rights of companies in the private sector, I would potentially be suggesting it, but I do not. I think it would be an act of genius beyond me to come up with a legislative regime that impacts in the private sector. I do understand that process. However, I think it does indicate an acknowledgement that, even on government-controlled projects, the protection of subcontractors and getting their payments has been insufficient. If that were not the case, we would not be debating the bill before the house. We would not be on the third version of attempting to deliver greater security. It is absolutely the case that the protections given from a government perspective, particularly for departments and government trading enterprises in the oversight of major projects, have not been sufficient. Members might think that is just my opinion, but, luckily, I have a bit of support on that. Members should be aware of Report 4: 2022–23: Payments to Subcontractors Working on State Government Construction Projects from the Office of the Auditor General. This was a very good report from our very good, hardworking Auditor General looking into how subcontractors are managing in government projects. I will not read the entire report because there would be no time to say all the other things I need to get to. I thought there were a couple of critical components of this on page 5 in the Auditor General's overview. It states:
While the three audited entities used PBAs,—
we found their administration of the accounts was done without due scepticism as there was little or no checking of the information provided by head contractors.

If members want a line from an Auditor General's report that kind of defines the issue, I think it is precisely that. I think that scepticism should be central to all our reviews of things. Scepticism and cynicism are critically important to the role that we do. Any good auditor or any good scientist should be based in scepticism and cynicism. That is exactly what they are supposed to do. Every hypothesis should be tested and retested until it either is disproved or, after a period of time, cannot be disproved so that everybody largely has to accept that it is probably valid until sometime down the track when it is all disproven a third time. That is critically important. Cynicism and scepticism are integral parts of every audit, including financial audits. They should always be looking for what goes wrong. I think it is absolutely true. Part of the problem is that proponents, be they government or private sector, looking to deliver a project are generally not looking for problems, are they? Let us say that the newly minted Minister Caddy is in charge of something large in infrastructure or transport—building a new massive road—and the parliamentary secretary comes along and says, "I've just got this report from the department. It looks like it's going badly. The subcontractors aren't getting paid." Who would want to be that person? Whoever is the purchaser generally does not want to hear about the problems that go on, although one would think that they would. It is the classic thing of management, is it not? The classic thing of management is to know about the problem so that something can be done about it and it can learn from it and fix it, but how often does that not happen? How often is that swept under the table and ignored? I probably do not even have to mention the problems the government has had that it swept under the table in recent years. Members just have to look at the answers we get to parliamentary questions to know that that is a standard operating procedure.
Hon Stephen Dawson : Outrageous.
Hon Dr Steve Thomas : That is a standard operating procedure.

It is obviously very difficult. We have a problem when government departments say, "It's all right. We know we are in good hands." The problem with government departments is that nobody wants to rock the boat. When the Auditor General says that there was not enough—I will make sure I use the correct word—"scepticism" in the review of these contract processes, I am absolutely certain that that is the case. I would be astounded if the public service was there looking for problems. I think it is probably more likely to be found in the private sector. It is possibly also more likely to turn into something a bit vicious. Lawyers at 50 paces is an interesting concept, Leader of the House. As I said earlier, there are companies that make their money by suing proponents. In my view, there are companies that have made billions of dollars around the world. Investment companies—many of them I am aware of coming out of America, but other places as well—make their money purchasing at-risk or poor projects and look for a way to sue the proponents, preferably governments, for breach of contract or some sort of failure of outcome. That is how they make billions. The situation is that there are companies out there that are pirates. I used that word in an online article many years ago about companies purchasing components of energy in Collie. They literally come in and buy a stranded or failing asset in order to sue a government to make a profit out of it. It absolutely happens. It is that complexity of having this argument with a company that knows full well that it is going into it to be litigious. It is incredibly difficult. The scepticism required of government is unfortunately not there. This report goes on to state:

Concerningly, incomplete and erroneous head contractor statutory declarations were accepted without follow up. Making a false statutory declaration is a serious offence and may be a warning sign about other compliance problems that entities must promptly address.

Holy mackerel! False statutory declarations should be more than a warning sign; they should be grounds for termination of a contract. It is much more complicated than that. Like I say, it is not just me. The Auditor General of Western Australia raised concerns about this. Bear in mind that this is obviously the 2022–23 report, the fourth report. I highly recommend it to members. For members who have not had the opportunity to read it and new members who were not here, it is absolutely worth a look.

I would like to quote from page 8 of the report. This is in relation to what was, at the time, the implementation of project bank accounts, which was the stepping stone that the McGowan government originally introduced to try to improve the system. It says:

However, principals will retain oversight through contractual arrangements. As a matter of course, state agencies are expected to require head contractors to facilitate third-party viewing access with the financial institution where the trust account is established.

The expectation is that when state agencies, be they government trading enterprises or departments, appoint a head contractor to a project, they will facilitate third-party viewing access. Someone will have to look over them—at the very least, hopefully, the Auditor General. The department or the GTE themselves should be overlooking that and as the hardworking Auditor General of Western Australia said, they are not doing that very well. Apparently this approach balances flexibility for contractors with transparency for government agencies, ensuring payments remain visible, accountable and properly safeguarded. Well, does it? I think that is where we have got to with this particular piece of legislation. I am an overwhelming optimist, Deputy President. Sorry, I just gave you a promotion there, Acting President. I am an overwhelming optimist. I am very hopeful—
Hon Dan Caddy : I thought you were a cynic.

heading: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
subject: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
parts: I remind members what is being acquired. The corridor is already publicly owned. The government seeks to buy commercial interests in the network with roughly 23 years remaining under the current lease. Brookfield has operated the business for many years and could now receive a substantial payment for its remaining interest. That makes it even more important to understand how the price is figured out. The minister says the government will only proceed if the transaction is financially prudent. I would expect nothing less and I think this place would expect nothing less. Saying those words is not a test that Parliament can apply; we need to know what the test actually is.

I have no doubt that the minister will spend some time reminding us that the original lease was entered into by the Liberal–National government in 2000. She has never been shy about bringing it up. There were reasons the decision was made, including Westrail's financial position at the time. There are also problems with how the arrangement worked in practice and those problems have been examined by the Auditor General and Parliament. I am not going to pretend that every aspect of the old lease has worked well, but that argument only gets us so far. Labor has been in government since 2017. The Minister for Transport has had that responsibility for the entirety of that time.

People using this railway are entitled to ask what has actually been done during the last nine years. Access charges have been disputed for years, as have maintenance standards, investment and the difficulties faced by businesses that want to get more freight onto rail. These issues did not appear overnight. They did not appear in 2025 or 2024. They were not discovered at the last election. The government has had the capacity to invest in specific projects. It has been able to work with the lessee. It has made changes to the access framework. When the minister says buying the business is the answer, I want to know exactly which obstacle that purchase removes. That leaves a simple question: What can the minister do after the buyback that she cannot do today? She also needs to explain why the other tools available to government have not delivered the improvements that industry has been asking for.

This is not something that we fix merely by changing ownership. Members will notice a trend in that statement throughout this contribution. If the price of using the railway remains too high or the service is not reliable, freight customers will make other choices. They will go elsewhere. I believe we should be able to come back to Parliament in five years' time and say whether changes have made things more competitive, whether more freight is on rail and whether the condition of the network has actually improved. Without those clear benchmarks, there is no fair way to judge whether the government has delivered what it is promising.

There is another reason I am reluctant to give the government a free pass on this bill and that is the way these powers will be exercised. The existing lease has already been the subject of criticism over poor transparency and oversight. As I mentioned earlier, the Auditor General and a parliamentary inquiry raised concerns about how the network was maintained and how much information was available to Parliament and to the broader public. We ought to learn from that experience. Under clause 29, certain commercially sensitive information can be removed from published material and the freight business need not be included in the Public Transport Authority's annual operation plan. That is important. Clause 30 provides an exemption from Infrastructure Western Australia's processes. Under clause 44, key ministerial orders will be gazetted but will not be subsidiary legislation subject to the usual disallowance process.

There may be commercial or legal reasons for some of those arrangements; I accept that, but there is a difference between protecting and negotiating a position and asking Parliament to look the other way. There is a big difference between those things. The government is seeking broad powers to acquire and reorganise a business that could involve a substantial amount of taxpayer money—a very substantial amount of taxpayer money. A final decision on the transaction is expected to be made by cabinet without a separate vote in this chamber. Before a deal is finalised, Parliament should know what opportunity it will have to scrutinise the proposed arrangements. Once the deal is complete, the public should be able to see the purchase price, the liabilities assumed by the state and the investment commitments made, subject to genuinely necessary commercial protections—I understand that. Any new operator should also face clear maintenance obligations with reporting on whether the network is actually performing better. Those arrangements should be settled before another long-term agreement is signed, especially with the option for 99 years.

heading: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
subject: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
parts: Mr Mark Folkard : Rail lines stopped carrying freight. More freight went to our roads and now another generation of Western Australian taxpayers face the job of bringing a strategic network back under public control. That is the Liberal–National government's legacy!

In 2000, the Court Liberal–National government privatised Westrail freight businesses and leased the state freight network for 49 years. Let me say that again: it leased it for 49 years. It was not for four years or 10 years, but for 49 years. The state received $292 million for the network lease and a further $294 million for the Westrail freight business itself. Together, that is about $587 million. That sounds like a lot of money, but this was back in 2000. Here is a number that should make every Western Australian angry. Just 12 years later, the Auditor General said that the replacement cost of the rail freight network had already surpassed $5 billion. That was in 2012. It is now 2026 and I suggest that that valuation could be as much as $10 billion based on the numbers there.

I will use the 2012 figures. Replacing the strategic rail network would have cost over $5 billion and we leased it for $292 million. Seriously? Sorry, I should say the opposition leased it, not us. Remember that. That is what short-term thinking looks like: take the money, take the announcement and, if we look at the clowns opposite, take the photo and then spend the proceeds. They are good at that. Here's the kicker. They left someone else to deal with what comes next—

The Acting Speaker: Sorry, member for Mindarie. I might just clarify, because there were some comments in my left ear. The distinction that has been drawn here by the Leader of the House is that the comments were not directed at particular individuals. It was more broadly about a party and a government's ideological position. Thank you.

Mr Mark Folkard : Where were we? Today we are dealing with what comes next. We are trying to bring the network back under government control. Members may ask why. It is because rail is too important to Western Australia to simply leave its future to a commercial calculation. It carries our grain, our minerals and our fertiliser. It connects regional industries with our ports. It keeps heavy freight off our roads. It is basic economic infrastructure. We have learned a very expensive lesson: a government should not sell a monopoly and then expect the public interest to magically appear to look after itself. The Auditor General sounded warnings about this years ago.

The grain lines degraded. I know this because when I was in Wagin, the amount of trains that had to be walked through the town because of the state of the rail network was significant. There are two tier 3 grain lines that have already been placed into care and maintenance. Without further government funding, another two face the same fate. Then there is the extraordinary problem that the successful bidder made an additional $400 million investment commitment as part of its tender process but that commitment was never put in the final lease. There is no clear record explaining why $400 million was not properly put into the lease. How did that happen? I am an old copper. Members know I am. Something smells rotten there. If I was to go back and look at the times, I would be very interested to see who was paying who when that occurred. How did that mysteriously disappear off the lease? I am sorry; something is crook there.

How does a government hand over control of a strategic asset for 49 years without making it absolutely certain that the investment needed to protect that infrastructure is nailed down? That did not happen. That is not clever government and that is not good asset management, and Western Australians are entitled to ask why we are now trying to repair the consequences. There is an even more basic problem. The performance standards themselves were weak. The Auditor General found that the unusual maintenance standards were effectively based on the condition on the rail back in 2000. What does that mean? The lease runs until 2049, but these standards of maintenance could leave us with infrastructure measured against requirements set half a century earlier. In plain language, we sold it in 2000, and in 2049, the maintenance standards will be based on what they were back in 2000. Seriously? Western Australia will not stand still for 50 years. Our population grows. Our mines grow. Our grain production changes. Our ports change. Technology changes. The freight tasks change. Our economy changes. We have locked our strategic infrastructure into a long-term commercial arrangement that has stopped our ability to respond. That is the trap of privatisation. If a government sells a public asset today, future governments will inherit that contract. Mr Speaker, I want to put it in very simple language: they took the money and we inherited the problem. We are now working to bring our railway back.

Today, the Cook Labor government is progressing the process to bring freight rail back under public control. The government has established a process involving Transport and Treasury. Negotiations have been pursued with Arc Infrastructure. This legislation is being progressed to create a legal framework that could allow the network to be returned to public control. Why would we go through that? It is because we have learned what happens when a government loses control of strategic infrastructure. The Minister for Transport and Major Infrastructure put the problem clearly to this place: the government may technically own the land and the network underneath the lease, but it does not have the control it needs. If a government wants to upgrade a line, it has to negotiate. The operator has us over a barrel. If a new industry wants to start, it has to negotiate. Again, it has got us over a barrel. If the government wants to make a decision because it is good for the whole Western Australian economy, it has to deal with a private commercial arrangement. The difference is that a private company will ask, "Does it make commercial sense for us?" In plain language, they ask, "What are we going to get out of it?" A government must ask, "Does this make sense for Western Australia?" That is not always the same question. One is about driving what is good for the business's pocket and the other is about what is better for the state of Western Australia. There is a big difference there. Those questions also do not always produce the same answer. A rail line may not produce enough profit in itself, but keeping the rail line open might save millions of dollars in road maintenance costs and keep thousands of truck movements off regional WA roads. It might support our farmers. It might support a new mine. It might support a new industry that is yet to be developed. It might connect a port. To members opposite, it might make a regional town economically viable.

heading: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
subject: Rail Freight System (Acquisition and Reorganisation) Bill 2026
parts: For regional communities, this legislation must ultimately be judged by practical outcomes. The government has argued that returning the freight rail network to public control will help support industry, reduce transport costs and improve the use of rail. Those are all worthwhile objectives, but there needs to be a clear plan for achieving them. Across the state, our producers and businesses need dependable freight connections and competitive transport options. Our community also needs the government to properly maintain the roads that continue to carry substantial heavy freight. Public ownership will not automatically shift freight from roads to rail. That will depend on access, pricing, infrastructure investment and whether rail services meet the practical requirements of industry. There is little value in spending a substantial sum to acquire the network if the result is simply a change of ownership without meaningful improvements in how freight moves. The acquisition should therefore be accompanied by clear objectives and measurable outcomes. Regional industries need to know how the government intends to improve freight access, support network investment and maintain commercial efficiency. Also, taxpayers should be able to judge whether their promised benefits are actually being delivered.

There is one further safeguard that I believe is essential. Once any acquisition is complete, the government should provide Parliament with a full account of the transaction. That should include the purchase consideration, the financing arrangements and liabilities assumed, and the anticipated cost of operating and maintaining the network. There should also be an independent review of the transaction's governance and compliance, with an appropriate role for the Auditor General. That review would help establish whether the government followed proper process and whether the transaction was undertaken consistently with the public interest. Of course, a review after the event cannot replace proper controls before the agreement is signed, and we need both. We need strong financial safeguards before the acquisition and transparent reporting afterwards. That is not an unreasonable expectation for a transaction of this importance. I support the intention of the rail freight bill and I see the potential benefits of returning this important infrastructure to public control. For regional Western Australia, a better freight rail system could support our industries, strengthen supply chains and reduce pressure on our roads.

These are all outcomes worth pursuing, but this Parliament has a responsibility to look beyond the intention of the legislation to consider how the powers it creates will be exercised. We do not yet have a publicly established purchase price, a complete account of the financial liabilities or a clear expectation of every safeguard that will govern the final decision, so I am asking the government to commit to an independent evaluation, a clearly defined maximum financial exposure, appropriate parliamentary scrutiny of any substantial commitment and full disclosure, and an independent review once the transaction is completed. These requirements should not prevent a responsible purchase; they should help ensure that any purchase is responsible.

parts: Of course, not all of those 18 services are fully operational. parts: Dr Jen shared that she was a child in care. She said the course of her life changed when she was on her way to a careers fair and a youth worker said to her, "What are you thinking? heading: Alcoa and South32-Alumina royalties
subject: Alcoa and South32—Alumina royalties
parts: It is a bargain struck between the state and a proponent that is then ratified by Parliament. The whole point of a state agreement is to provide certainty for very large, very capital intensive projects that operate over decades and they are the cornerstone of the Western Australian economy. Government gets commitments and it gets decades-long investments into our economy and our communities and the proponent gets certainty about the rules under which that investment is made and the rules that that investment will be subjected to. That matters when we talk about the royalty review provisions in the state agreements that the member for Nedlands is referring to, because these agreements provide for periodic reviews of alumina royalties, but they do not provide for automatic increases to the royalty rate. A review is not a power for government to simply write into an agreement whatever royalty rate the government of the day decides—whatever it likes. In the Alcoa agreements, in fact, the royalty is expressly said to be subject to review by the parties, not to review by the government but by the parties—the proponent and the government. With Worsley, again the royalty is subject to review by the parties with agreements specifying the matters that they must have regard to. Where there are disputes under that agreement, there are arbitration mechanisms. It is not just a matter of simple enforcement. The dispute goes to arbitration.

Saying in this motion that the government has simply failed to enforce a higher royalty rate fundamentally misunderstands the instruments that we are dealing with and it is not the first time that we have heard members of the other side of the chamber, the people who are members or have been members of the party of Charles Court, misunderstand the nature of state agreements in this chamber. There is always a bigger question that we should ask as members when we are scrutinising state agreements. It should not just be about the percentage royalty rate. We have to ask: What is the total value of the bargain? What is the total value of the state agreement to the people of Western Australia? Of course royalty revenue matters. As the member for Nedlands said, Western Australia should receive fair value for the resources that are owned by the people of Western Australia but the public return from these projects is not just measured by that percentage. It is measured by decades of jobs that have been created, by local contractors and supply chains, by capital investment, by skills and apprenticeships that have been provided over many, many years, and by the economic activity that, in the case of Alcoa, flows through a series of regional communities around Wagerup, Waroona and Yarloop. The Auditor General found in her review of state agreement projects that all of those matters should rightly be taken into account as being part of the total value of a state agreement. That is the test that we should be applying in this chamber ourselves.

That leads me to a point about how you maximise value from a state agreement because maximising value from a state agreement is not just about collecting the most royalties. There is an important principle behind our royalty system. We should be encouraging, to the extent we can, value-adding to resources here in Western Australia. It is a key objective of this Cook Labor government. Our ordinary mineral royalty system already recognises the degree of processing of a product. The more processing and value-adding undertaken here the lower, generally, that the rate of royalty becomes. There is a reason for that. We do not want to create an incentive for someone to dig something out of the ground and ship it overseas in its least processed form. We want refining, we want manufacturing, we want jobs and we want more of that value being captured here in Western Australia, and setting the right royalty is important to that.

heading: Westport Bill 2026
subject: Westport Bill 2026
parts: Several members asked: Why do we need a new authority for Westport? The reason is the size and scope of the project. It is a once-in-a-generation infrastructure project. It has distinct commercial, engineering and delivery profiles. A dedicated authority will provide specialist capability, a single point of accountability and the ability to engage effectively with national and international markets. At the same time, setting up a dedicated authority will allow Fremantle port to continue to focus on doing what it needs to do, which is support trade through the existing port.

Some questions were raised about accountability, procurement and financial powers. The exclusions from the Public Sector Management Act and the Procurement Act are designed to provide a fit-for-purpose delivery model, not to reduce oversight. The authority will operate under a tailored procurement framework that emphasises competition, probity, transparency and value for money. In addition, it will remain subject to board oversight, ministerial oversight, the Financial Management Act, the Treasurer's instructions, the Auditor General's scrutiny and parliamentary reporting. On financing, while the bill enables borrowing, borrowing is not intended to be the primary funding model. Any financing arrangements will remain subject to the Expenditure Review Committee and Treasury oversight and the state's broader fiscal framework. Likewise, significant transactions will be subject to additional scrutiny under thresholds to be prescribed by regulations and subject to parliamentary oversight. Questions were also raised about costs in the business case. The Westport business case released in November 2024 estimated a project cost of $7.2 billion. As with any infrastructure project of this scale, costs and assumptions will continue to be refined.

Of course, as part of this, we are also in the stages of delivering the defence precinct. One of the key parts of the work that we are doing is looking at the total scope of the works, such as sequencing the work where we can achieve some economies of scale by not undertaking two sets of work. We are looking at all things, but that is particularly the case on the maritime side, such as breakwaters and dredging.

Mr Adam Hort : The Public Sector Management Act has a range of protections for staff, but it also has integrity requirements as well, which are really important. What will guide the authority's arrangements given that staff will not be considered part of the public sector? How will the authority manage staff and what integrity arrangements will be put in place?

Ms Rita Saffioti : Although staff are not employed under the PSMA, the bill imposes a governance and integrity framework. Minimum standards for the workplace will be set after consultation with the Public Sector Commissioner—strict duties equivalent to corporate directors' duties, part 8; ministerial direction and information rights, part 10; and full financial accountability through the Financial Management Act 2006 and the Auditor General Act 2006. These measures replicate the safeguards that are found in public sector legislation.
Mr Adam Hort : What agility is being provided under this arrangement that does not exist under the Public Sector Management Act? In what way does it lack agility?

heading: Westport Bill 2026
subject: Westport Bill 2026
parts: I turn to the authority proposed by the bill. There is a sensible case for a dedicated delivery body. The Westport office currently sits within the Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure. Fremantle Ports is set up to operate and maintain an existing port and deliver projects within that operating environment. Constructing a new container port of this scale is a different undertaking entirely. It requires specialist commercial engineering, procurement and project delivery capability. Giving Fremantle Ports all the additional people and powers required would in practical terms create much of the same delivery organisation under another name.

The bill establishes the Westport Authority as an agent of the state. It will be outside of the public sector management framework while remaining subject to the Financial Management Act and the Auditor General Act. It will have a board appointed by the minister, commercial powers, borrowing powers subject to limits set by the Treasurer and the ability to enter into substantial transactions subject to the approval regime in part 10. That structure may provide the commercial speed that the project requires. It also places a greater responsibility on the government to show how public money will be protected and how Parliament will see what the authority is doing, and that is key.

Clause 178 exempts the authority from the Procurement Act 2020, consistent with the treatment of port authorities and other government trading enterprises, but the scale of the proposed program makes the authority's replacement arrangements very, very important. We will ask whether the authority intends to continue advertising opportunities through Tenders WA, what procurement rules it will adopt, how local content obligations will be applied, how conflicts will be managed and what information will be published about major contracts. The government has said the authority needs greater commercial agility, and I accept that a major project cannot require approval from two ministers every time it enters into a routine agreement. Agility cannot become an excuse for opacity; however, the public should be able to see the standards governing procurement, the delegations given to officers and the process for reporting contracts and variations.

heading: Essential services

parts: We know that across the board, at this time, under this government, about 10% of patients are now waiting 12 hours or more in emergency departments to receive the care that they need. At Fiona Stanley Hospital and Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital today, that was as much as 15%. What an appalling record of a government that has no-one else to blame but itself. We have five health ministers and the largest boom our state has ever seen. There is no previous government to blame. Surely, the government cannot blame winter. We have heard about strategies, reviews, taskforces, reforms and future projects, but what happens when someone arrives at the emergency department, calls an ambulance, waits for elective surgery or tries to access the mental health system? The experience tells a very different story. Ambulance ramping has not fallen. Wait times at EDs have not improved. Elective surgery lists have grown, and we have the worst nurse ratios in the nation. The 32 mental health reforms that were recommended some years ago have not been implemented or delivered as promised. Today, we saw another scathing report from the independent Auditor General, as well. The Auditor General exposed the serious failures in over $1 billion in health payments under this government's watch. Mr Basil Zempilas : A perfect storm!

Ms Libby Mettam : A perfect storm for fraud were the words delivered at the Auditor General briefing today. We heard that nearly $1 billion of taxpayers' money was being processed through a pathway the Auditor General says is not being effectively managed. The Auditor General found weak controls, payments without adequate supporting evidence, failures to follow procurement rules and an environment with an elevated risk of fraud and inappropriate payments. It sounds familiar. We have raised these issues before. Quite clearly, this government is not in any control of Health. What is also disappointing is that we have a government that simply does not care. We have pointed to the fact that health workers, nurses, doctors and allied health workers have now been waiting three years for the Your Voice in Health survey to resume. Despite a tender going out last September with 10 responses received, the Your Voice in Health survey rejected every applicant. We are now again seeing the voices and feedback of our valued health workers effectively shut down by a government that is not interested in that valuable feedback.

The last survey conducted under this government's watch showed that just 28% of health workers felt valued and respected. Only 25% of health workers believed that their organisation cared about their health and wellbeing, and 23% did not believe that those leading their organisation were honest. That was the feedback received from health workers last time. Instead of trying to fix these issues, what does the government do? It shuts down the survey, and we hear more excuses from the Minister for Health as to why.

The elective surgery waitlist has grown significantly by about 50%. Increasingly, the concern is those waiting above the clinical boundary. A waitlist of between 29,000 and 30,000 people is not a sign of success. It is not a sign of a government that is getting the basics right and delivering for the people of WA.

The child and adolescent mental health reform is one of the most disturbing examples of the government's inaction. The Auditor General's report was scathing and, after three years, only one of its 32 recommendations had been delivered. That is not a minor delay; it is a profound failure of execution.

We have other members who would like to speak, Acting Speaker, so I will leave my comments there. Quite clearly, this government is an absolute failure when it comes to the fundamentals of health, and Western Australian patients and health workers are paying the price.
