heading: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
subject: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
parts: I have also raised this issue. Even though we are talking about working with children checks, the element of child protection that I raised with the Fogliani reports flows into this. There has been a lack of progress reports. We have annual reports, but there have been no progress reports along the way. Recommendations have been made about these things and have been accepted in principle, but we are still sitting on them and not prioritising them at all.

Child protection is very easy to discuss at a distance. I know that Hon Rod Caddies has often relayed some of these stories. I do not think we truly comprehend the magnitude of some of the issues that have been raised on the floor of this chamber, including by Hon Nick Goiran. It is much harder to dismiss it when we hear from a person who is in that situation or who has followed this for a long period. Often, people do not expect something extraordinary. It is as simple as saying, "We are raising an issue. There is a gap in the system. These recommendations have been accepted to mitigate that gap. Can we now move in a timely manner to implement them?" That is why the timing of this bill baffles me. We have known about the weaknesses in the working with children screening system for such a long time. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse identified them. The Working with Children Checks Report made 36 recommendations, 34 of which apply to state governments. The government accepted 30 of those in principle. Those recommendations included the establishment of a national database, which is what we are now seeing. That was 11 years ago. Concerns were also identified by the Auditor General in 2014 and again in 2019. We are hardly short on warnings here. Over the last couple of years, there have been horrific reminders of what is at stake. But, no, the wellbeing and safety of children is apparently paramount.

In Queensland, a childcare worker faced court over allegations. In the case of Ashley Griffith, he was jailed for life after sexually abusing nearly 70 girls while working in childcare centres. In WA alone, there have been 109 investigations into alleged sexual abuse in childcare centres since 2020, with 97 resulting in no further action. Ten per cent of allegations of grooming and sexual abuse result in a ban from the sector. Former WA teacher Kurt Charlton was sentenced to more than six years in prison after 27 instances, and I could go on. In May this year, WA police charged a 19-year-old basketball referee with 22 alleged offences. I am not suggesting that those offences only happened because there was no national working with children check, but, again, they are reminders that every weakness in screening, information sharing, reporting and oversight has to be addressed as a matter of priority. If there is a gap in the system designed to keep children safe, unfortunately, as we have seen from all these cases, somebody will find it. As we said during debate on the surrogacy legislation, there are gaps. We need working with children checks, criminal checks and security checks to ensure that these kids are safe.

These are substantial issues. They go to the scope of the safeguard itself. I am not suggesting that every single proposal in the consultation paper should automatically become law, but they do have to be examined carefully, and they do need to be prioritised. If the government has deliberately separated this part of phase 2 because national recognition had to be dealt with first, then I think we are entitled to ask this government when the rest of phase 2 will be forthcoming. Which categories of child-related work will be reconsidered? Which exemptions will be reviewed? What has the government concluded from the consultation that it expressly relied on when answering my question last November? This is perhaps something to delve into later, during Committee of the Whole.

After a decade of reviews and reforms, is it not reasonable for this Parliament to have a clear picture of how this government is prioritising child protection and child safety? I reiterate that the royal commission was a decade ago. The first report from the Auditor General was almost 12 years ago, and the follow-up was seven years ago. Phase 1 implementation was three years ago. At some point, we have to move beyond saying that we have accepted another recommendation or that we appreciate or take notice of another red flag. When is the time for action?

Unfortunately, the question of delay extends beyond this bill and seems to be a pattern in this space. Last November, the Auditor General reported on Western Australia's implementation of the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, and I will read from it. The Auditor General's report said:

WA is lagging behind other jurisdictions in completing this important work. Nearly eight years after committing to doing so, WA still does not have legislation mandating compliance with the National Principles.
Nearly eight years after WA committed to mandating the National Principles and creating independent oversight it remains one of only two jurisdictions yet to finish this work.
How embarrassing is that, Deputy President? The Auditor General also wrote:

The State's slow progress to implement the National Principles is disappointing, especially given recent publicised failings in childcare that highlight the heartbreaking fact that children continue to experience harm.
They are quotes from the Auditor General and significant findings.

The government has announced the Ombudsman as the independent oversight body. Great! These are positive steps, but let us be under no illusions here. The Auditor General also made it very clear that "this vital function cannot start until resourcing is confirmed and relevant legislation passed".

As any person would, I asked the government about this once again in June. I asked when this oversight scheme would become fully operational and what would be the specific enforcement powers of the Ombudsman. When is this going to happen? It was announced. There was a big kerfuffle about it, so when is it actually going to happen? The response was that an implementation plan was being developed, including stakeholder engagement and timeframes. More importantly, the government said that the timeframe for this scheme becoming operational and specific enforcement powers were being considered as part of this process. Even there, we still do not know when this scheme will become operational or what enforcement powers the Ombudsman will have. Is this really the attitude of the government when it comes to the wellbeing and protection of children? It is paramount.

It is nothing new. It is not that things are not happening. I appreciate that things are happening. Reviews are being conducted and recommendations are being accepted, but I often find myself at a place where I think: But then what? It is almost as if so much happens, so much is accepted and so much is recommended—then what?

We saw something similar in June this year when the Auditor General reported on the transformation of the child and adolescent mental health services. Again, the government accepted 32 recommendations from the ministerial task force. Four years later, one had been completed, 26 remain in progress, and five have not even been started yet. The Auditor General found repeatedly changing governance arrangements, inadequate accountability and the exclusion of key stakeholders from part of this reform process—that is quite scathing—and 12 of the original 32 recommendations had not even been included in the original implementation plan.

I appreciate that this is not directly talking about the working with children check issue, but it is relevant to the broader question of how we deal with recommendations intended to protect children. There comes a point at which good intentions are just not enough, Deputy President. The same question of consistency arose with the Civil Liability Amendment (Child Sexual Abuse Actions) Bill 2025. As introduced, the bill only applied to religious practitioners and institutions. The government argued that it needed to act urgently, following the High Court's decision in Bird v DP, yet every other jurisdiction in Australia that has legislated in this area has extended vicarious liability beyond religious institutions, something clearly outlined by Hon Nick Goiran. Queensland is the only jurisdiction yet to legislate. We are so behind the eight ball on this matter. I have said before that as a Christian, I have no interest in shielding churches or Christian organisations from proper accountability when children have been harmed. The royal commission exposed those terrible failures, and those failures need to be acknowledged and dealt with, and they are. If the principle is that an institution entrusted with children should be accountable when it fails them, surely we can appreciate that that principle has to apply consistently. The harm to a child does not change according to whether that institution is religious, secular, private or government run. Again, as we know, working with children check cards are important, but they are just one element. This is part of a broader system approach. That is why the culture around these systems and matters needs to change. An organisation can have the right policies, procedures and screening requirements in place and still fail a child if concerns are dismissed, if there are gaps and if we, as decision-makers, fail to prioritise these matters when they come up. Ultimately, the test happens when somebody speaks up. We have seen a plethora of examples of people, families, organisations, Auditors General and coroners speaking up, and it is just falling on deaf ears.

The people serving in this area of child protection are extraordinary, selfless and amazing. I know that they only want the best for the people who they serve. Many carry enormous responsibility in the work that they do. Very often, they are the people who notice first when something is wrong. We have an absolute obligation to make sure that the systems around them are helping them and taking note and action rather than hindering that process. In fact, I even raised this in my budget reply speech. The government is spending $690 million on child protection, including $421 million on out-of-home care, and, again, there is additional support for foster and grandparent carers. That reveals the scale of responsibility that we are talking about here. Over the past decade, the number of children in out-of-home care has increased by more than a thousand. Over a longer period, the need for foster care has risen substantially. The needs and complexity in this space have risen significantly. Of course, a lot of this eventually lands with people and within the systems. It applies to schools, childcare centres, organisations, government departments and churches. It is a whole-of-community approach.

My view of humanity begins with the understanding that a person's value does not depend on how powerful or independent they are or what they can contribute. A person's value is absolutely important and their worth is inherent. Because children have so little control of their circumstances and the systems around them, they rely on us to be able to be that leading decision-maker. We make these decisions and we prioritise these things for them. It is a huge responsibility that we cannot take lightly. If we are entrusted, whether in Parliament or government, we carry that obligation and that responsibility.

Passing this bill is important, but I believe the work is far from done. The remainder of phase 2 still needs to be dealt with. The Ombudsman's oversight role still needs the legislation and resourcing around it. The national principles are not yet fully implemented. There are still recommendations flowing on from the royal commission that remain unfinished. I will not stray too far, but I again come back to Coroner Fogliani's reports and recommendations, which are such good reports with feedback and recommendations that are waiting to be implemented so that the wellbeing and safety of children is looked after. The Auditor General continues to identify delays and implementation problems that are affecting the most vulnerable children.

Before I finish, I think it is reasonable to ask the government: Where to from here? I would like to see it take four steps. Firstly, give us a clear timetable for the remainder of phase 2. Secondly, bring forward the legislation necessary for the Ombudsman to undertake the independent child safety oversight role. Resource them and make sure that that is absolutely ready to go. Thirdly, give Parliament a clear account of which royal commission recommendations remain to be implemented. Which recommendations are still outstanding? I just cannot believe how difficult it has been over the last 18 months just to get basic information such as what recommendations have been implemented and when they will be implemented. I understand that multiple departments are involved in some of these complex cases, but how hard is it to know which recommendations have been implemented in a specific area and which ones remain outstanding? Why is it so difficult to get this information? Fourthly, it would be fantastic for progress to be reported. Tell us what remains, who is responsible and when it is expected to be done, and then come back and tell us whether it was done. It is a team effort. This is ultimately what prevention looks like so that we are not constantly responding to a crisis—another example and another case. We want to start avoiding those situations.

heading: Animal protection
subject: Animal protection
parts: Hon Amanda Dorn : It is about institutional design, minister.

As legislators, we understand the principle of institutional design in every other area of government. Good governance requires more than good intentions; it requires accountability, transparency and independence where competing interests exist. This is why we have an Auditor General, this is why we have a Corruption and Crime Commissioner and this is why we have a Commissioner for Children and Young People. These independent officers exist because Parliament recognised that some responsibilities are just way too important to be left without independent oversight, but when it comes to animal wellbeing, our state is falling behind.

This motion does not ask the government to invent something new; it asks the government to catch up. In 2023, an Inspector General of Animal Welfare and Live Animal Exports was established federally—a clear acknowledgement that oversight of animal welfare cannot sit entirely within the same agency responsible for promoting the industries being overseen. Ahead of the 2025 federal election, Labor promised to expand that role further to include oversight of export abattoirs. South Australia has gone further again. Its new Animal Welfare Act, passed in 2025, formally recognises animals as living beings capable of feeling and experiencing positive and negative emotions. This is a foundational principle that reshapes how welfare decisions are made and enforcement prioritised.

heading: Kate Savage
subject: Kate Savage
parts: The final report was handed down in March 2022. The taskforce proposed a vision and a whole range of strategies, purposes and principles. It put forward key foundational changes that would help to address situations like Kate's family faced, including fundamental requirements about involving parents in decision-making. It proposed new models of care and multiple actions that can be taken. We heard in question time just recently, in a question asked by Hon Philip Scott, that $235 million has been put specifically into this transformational project.

The Auditor General and her team provided a briefing yesterday on the performance audit that was done of the Mental Health Commission's work. The Auditor General's report is titled Progress of the Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health System Transformation Program. The Auditor General has this report as a blueprint and has done an audit that was handed down in June, four years after the final report from the ministerial taskforce. The Final Report – Ministerial Taskforce into Public Mental Health Services for Infants, Children and Adolescents aged 0–18 years in WA had 32 recommendations, all of which were accepted by government. Every single recommendation was supported and accepted by government in the beginning of 2022. Here we are in June 2026; $235 million has been invested in this, yet the findings are that one recommendation has been adopted. Only one recommendation out of 32 has been met. This was planned to be a nine-year project. It is one-third of the way in. We are four years from when the government accepted all the recommendations, and yet only one recommendation has been properly implemented.

The Auditor General's report goes through this in detail in quite kind language. It can only be described as not only a lack of implementation but also a very significant and serious lack of planning, even. When we look at the comments and the findings made, we find that lives are at stake from the significant mental health issues of children and young people. We know that suicide is the leading cause of death for our young people in WA. We have this significant amount of work, so what would we expect to see four years later, three years into this project? We would certainly not expect to see the picture painted by the Auditor General. There is a vast difference between what the Auditor General expected to see at this point of the process and what has actually been provided. In plain English, the basic expectations have not been met. There are 32 recommendations; only one recommendation has been met. These issues are not being focused on seriously enough. They are not being taken seriously. There is no plan. There is no collection of baseline data. No funding is allocated specifically to the implementation of all this. There is no monitoring, and there is no accountability.

It is very interesting to look at the timelines for the development of the structures that were supposed to implement this. For six months, there was a working group, then it disappeared for 13 months. There has been a new working group since February 2024, and that new working group still does not have any terms of reference. How can the working group even track, monitor or consider what changes have been made if it does not even have the baseline requirement of terms of reference? It is being said that it is advisory and consultative. Who is actually implementing these recommendations? Who is actually taking up all the recommendations, research and data? Someone needs to be held accountable for the fact that millions of dollars have been spent but no outcomes are being implemented—sorry, one outcome has been achieved.

The Auditor General's team has done a deep dive into this issue. Its report has two recommendations. I do not have time to read them out, but I will summarise them. I would summarise the first recommendation as saying that the Mental Health Commission needs to make a plan to implement the recommendations and allocate the responsibility to do so to someone. The second recommendation is to follow the plan. This is not good enough. More needs to be done to deal with this.

heading: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
subject: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
speakerRaw: Hon Nick Goiran (Leader of the Opposition) (3:49 pm)
parts: It has been reported that 12 childcare centres in our own state are set to close, in part due to collapsing parental confidence in the wake of the childcare predator exposé. Who could blame them?

The article that I referred to earlier from 3 May also highlights the Western Australian Government's failings in delivering another key recommendation of the royal commission—the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations. The Auditor General here in WA—the independent Auditor General—reports to Parliament. She undertook a performance audit into Western Australia's progress to implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations in November 2025, and it revealed the government's lack of progress. I quote from that report, titled WA's progress to Implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations (arising from the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse). Amongst other things in that report, the Auditor General in her overview says:

WA is lagging behind other jurisdictions in completing this important work. Nearly eight years after committing to do so, WA still does not have legislation mandating compliance with the National Principles.
Later on, the Auditor General says:

The State's slow progress to implement the National Principles is disappointing, especially given recent publicised failings in childcare that highlight the heartbreaking fact that children continue to experience harm.

It would be a good use of members' time over the winter recess to spend perhaps half an hour—I do not think it would require more than that—to consider what legislation has been passed so far in this 42nd Parliament. What has been the priorities of the Cook Labor government in the 42nd Parliament with respect to legislation? The matters that members will read during that half-hour exercise, if they choose to undertake it during the winter recess, have all been prioritised ahead of this, despite the fact that this has been called for for a decade.

During the Auditor General's audit, on 24 October 2025 the government announced the Ombudsman as the independent oversight body for organisations engaged in child-related work. There was a media release pushed by the government, titled "New scheme to strengthen safety for WA children."
The Auditor General's report stated:
While this is welcome progress, this vital function cannot start until resourcing is confirmed and relevant legislation passed.

When the Auditor General was undertaking this audit into how the government is progressing in implementing the recommendations from the royal commission, this government—again, disingenuously—pushes out a media release in October. I recall it well. At the time, the Minister for Child Protection was proudly saying: "Look at what the Cook Labor government is doing—we have a new scheme to strengthen safety for WA children". At the time, the Minister for Child Protection, very enthusiastically, said that the Ombudsman would be appointed to undertake this function.

The ordinary reader—the ordinary Western Australian citizen, the ordinary Western Australian voter—would have taken from that media release that the Ombudsman would be undertaking that work effective immediately. Was that the case? It was disingenuous, and it was called out by the Auditor General. That particular announcement in October by the Minister for Child Protection, which was presumably designed to somehow kibosh the audit that was being undertaken, was called out in the Auditor General's final report in November, a month later.
As I said, the Auditor General stated:

Interestingly, the other organisation that I had the opportunity to confer with was the Western Australian Local Government Association, because it also made a submission to the phase 2 reform consultation paper. I would also characterise its response to this bill as qualified approval. It certainly is supportive of the cross-jurisdictional checks, but it also says there are some missed opportunities for amendments to reflect contemporary local government service provisions that are not covered, including the variety of engagement local government staff and elected members have with children. The Western Australian Local Government Association also noted it is keenly awaiting implementation of the independent child safeguarding oversight body to handle complaints, as recommended by the royal commission. That is that role of the Ombudsman that I referred to earlier.

I did not have time then, so I will say now that in that public hearing undertaken by the Standing Committee on Public Administration, I asked the Ombudsman when this particular regime was expected to come into effect. A couple of members from that committee are now in the chamber so if I get this wrong, they will be in a position to correct me. My recollection is that the Ombudsman said that this would not happen until 2028. We have the Minister for Child Protection waving around a media release in October last year—why? It was because she and her department are under investigation by the Auditor General saying, "How are you going with the implementation of the royal commission's recommendations?" She disingenuously puts out this media release with social media et cetera to say, "I have appointed the Ombudsman to undertake this role", but when scrutinised and investigated further by the Standing Committee on Public Administration it becomes clear that nothing is happening. Why? No legislation is before the house and, in any event, it is not expected to happen until 2028. Nothing for the rest of 2026, nothing for 2027 and maybe—fingers crossed, hope to die—it will be in 2028. That is the level of priority that this government has given to child protection matters. It is simply not good enough.

heading: Public Education Endowment Repeal Bill 2025
subject: Public Education Endowment Repeal Bill 2025
parts: We know that for the past decade, the Public Education Endowment Trust has been largely dormant. In fact, I think 2013 was the last time any money was drawn from that trust as funding for educational purposes. It also has not acquired any land, nor has it undertaken any substantive activities beyond the minimal administrative and reporting requirements to keep the trust alive, so to speak. Another financial year's end is quickly approaching, so it is hugely advantageous to try to dissolve the trust to again avoid the expenditure, cost or time of unnecessary financial reporting, given the state of the trust. There is also broad recognition by all members who made a contribution that the trust's current structure is outdated and no longer fit for purpose. Of course, the intent of this bill is to modernise the approach and bring closure to an arrangement that is really historical but no longer aligns with our contemporary governance or education funding needs. Ending the trust in this existing form and directing the Public Education Endowment Trust's idle funds to education will allow us to honour the original purpose, which is supporting education through a much more effective and transparent mechanism.

On the second matter—the land valuation and delay of the bill—I want to make a few brief remarks. A number of members raised questions regarding the valuation of the land, known as the Knutsford land. At the time of the introduction of the bill last year, it relied on the audited valuation that was available in the 2023–24 PEET annual report, for which the Auditor General provided an unqualified audit opinion at the time. Further work has since been done to update that valuation in line with recommendations from the Auditor General that were tabled in Parliament after the introduction of the bill. The Auditor General found that the Landgate valuation of the trust's land did not demonstrate fair market value. In that regard, the trustees accepted the advice of the Auditor General and the independent valuation of $26.85 million was adopted by the trust in the 2024–25 annual report that was tabled in Parliament. It is important to note that there were no findings of any impropriety in relation to the valuation of the land by the Auditor General. This was a technical correction, which has now been resolved. Ensuring these matters were fully resolved before progressing the bill was critical to maintaining confidence in the valuation and financial arrangements.

Thirdly and lastly, I just want to make a few brief remarks on the application of funds after the dissolution, if this bill passes through Parliament. The most significant concerns that were raised during debate relate to the original proposal for trust moneys to be paid into the consolidated account rather than a dedicated special purpose account under the Financial Management Act 2006. I acknowledge the importance of ensuring that funds intended for education remain protected and used solely for that purpose. In response to the issues raised, I confirm that the fair and equivalent value of the Public Education Endowment Trust's assets will be held within the consolidated account—specifically, a Department of Treasury and Finance–administered provision—for distribution to support school maintenance and minor works projects. The Department of Treasury and Finance cannot transfer these funds to the Department of Education until the bill has been enacted. The PEET funds have been incorporated into the Department of Education's 2026–27 budget statements to ensure full transparency. Those statements clearly identify the allocation of $39.9 million for targeted school maintenance and minor works upgrades. Securing the funding through the budget process via a Treasury and Finance–administered provision removes the need to amend the repeal bill or establish a special purpose account—options that were examined but determined to introduce unnecessary bureaucracy and limit the efficient use of the funds. In fact, the amendment that was contemplated by the opposition would effectively mean a delay in the proceeds going to education because transference into a special account would require the sale of the land, which of itself could still be a lengthy process. Under this arrangement, having secured the money into the budget means that, as soon as the bill is passed, access to the full amount of money—the assets of the trust—will be available to education.

Mr Peter Rundle : The first question I have, and I think the minister did cover this a little in her speech, is about the current valuation of the trust's holdings. The minister spoke about the $39.9 million, derived, I think, from the Office of the Auditor General report. Can the minister provide a bit more clarity as to how that process took place? Ms Sabine Winton : The member is right: I did try to explain the timeline in terms of how the valuation changed from when the bill was first introduced in the last Parliament in 2023 or 2024. At the time of the introduction of the bill, the bill relied on the audited valuation available in the Public Education Endowment Trust's 2023–24 Annual Report. Further work has been done since then, which took some time. There was also a delay between bringing the bill back to Parliament in April 2025 and updating that valuation in line with the advice from the Auditor General's report, which was tabled in Parliament in December 2025. As I said, when the bill was introduced in April 2025, the Landgate valuation was $7.3 million, and this had been audited in that annual report and accepted by the Auditor General without qualification, albeit that concerns were raised. The Auditor General did make some general observations about land transfers but also made clear that these situations are complex and that values can differ depending on future use. I tried to emphasise that in the second reading and I guess I want to re-emphasise it here. Importantly, there was no qualified audit opinion, so the $7.3 million figure remained the best available and trusted value at the time. It was later clarified that this figure reflected DevelopmentWA's intended use of the land, not market value, as is standard. Following the Auditor General's recommendations, an independent valuation was commissioned, which found that the land was worth $26.9 million. This updated value is now fully reflected in PEET's latest annual report, which was tabled in December. Likewise, the budget limit in this year's state budget reflects that new valuation.

Mr Peter Rundle : I did have other questions about the guarantee that it will end up in education. Can the minister run that past me again? She spoke about it in her speech, but how will the Treasury–administered maintenance provision actually work in practice?

parts: Now I come to a time when I am looking at what we are doing with our budget. Bear in mind, a budget might be just three very complicated tomes with figures, but it is also setting a priority. It is setting a choice. It is setting a decision on how we are going to move forward. We have our money and our facilities, and we are now going to decide what deserves this money most. That which is least deserving will drop off the end because we cannot afford that. We have here a very clearly set out list of priorities, something we ought to be taking note of, and this is really what I want to speak about when I speak in depth about this current budget. As I said, it is a good budget as far as budgets go, but it will be interesting to see how far this budget actually meets the needs of the people we claim to represent.

That being said, I would like to move forward to talk about the first area, which is transparency. How can we see what is going on in our budget? We have the example—it is a very interesting example—of the Auditor General. I highly recommend that more of us attend the meetings with the Auditor General in this building; they seem to be very sparsely populated. The information that the Auditor General produces is very interesting and very important for us to be aware of. One of the areas on which the Auditor General was seeking information was some financial information from the government specifically on the Griffin Coal Ashurst engagement. The Auditor General requested information of the government that the government declined to produce. We have an Auditor General who is charged with ensuring that what is actually happening is measurable, verifiable and responsible, and the government that has engaged the Auditor General has then refused to supply the data needed to make an estimation. I think that in itself is a ground for concern. The Auditor General records that, without that information, she cannot assess whether the refusals were actually reasonable.

Of course, the condition was given that it is commercial-in-confidence. We heard this earlier in our discussions about question time, when very often questions are refused to be answered because of cabinet-in-confidence and issues with commerciality, and therefore the answer cannot be given. It is a very nice smokescreen or curtain that prevents us from accessing the data and seeing what is going on until a more appropriate time when the confidentiality is no longer necessary.

I find this troubling, because in the case of the Auditor General, the information that she deals with is then kept secure and secret. There is no widespread dissemination of secure information; it is used as an interpretation of what needs to be documented as part of her job—the job that we as a government have given her. This request was refused. I find that very challenging to accept, because it begs the question: Where else is government less than open about information about which it should be open? We as a people need to know what our government is actually doing, and if we are forbidden from finding out, if our ability to access the information and make a reasonable decision based on the information available is forbidden to us, we are basically kept in the dark, we are unable to make a rational, logical choice, we are unable to make a decision of what is necessary here, and, as a people, when we come to elect our government, we are denied the information we need to make a reasonable choice. I think that should trouble each and every one of us in this chamber.

The act that regulates this was assented to in late November 2022. It allowed the Auditor General to have access to information. It inserted new information-gathering powers over privileged and confidential material, with penalties to the government of $50,000 if we fail. It actually strengthened the hand of the Auditor General, and still the government refused to provide the information. I believe the act was passed but remains unproclaimed three and a half years on.

But the implication that ministers and parliamentary secretaries in this place do not understand their role as representatives of other ministers is, quite frankly, incorrect. As I said, we all read the questions before we answer them. There is a hive of activity to go through them. Certainly I and other ministers in this place have stood up and said we are not happy with the answer or that we will seek to get a more concise or clearer answer for the member the next day. The number of times we have to table information because so much detail has been asked is, again, evidence that we provide a lot of data in a short time, when it is asked for.

parts: Using this generous approach, our analysis is that this budget allocates just 0.57% to nature. Let us remember that this is a government that can find $270 million for a racetrack that no-one wants and can partner with the federal government to find $1.1 billion for just the first stage of the Anketell Road upgrade, spending $550 million of state funds to get this done, but when it comes to the critical work of the on-ground protection and restoration of WA's extraordinary natural environment, from the Kimberley to the Great Southern and everything in between, it can find only $303 million—just 0.57% of the budget. I am sure people will be aware that there is a push for the federal government to find 1% of the federal budget for nature. That equates to about $6 billion to $7 billion of the federal budget. That is a far greater sum, of course, than 1% of the state budget, but I also believe that it is on the very low end of what is needed. The fact is that two centuries of colonisation, land clearing and excessive extraction have put us in what can only be described as major nature debt. We should recognise this and invest in on-ground nature protection and restoration work as a matter of urgency and as a key priority.

So, what would the Greens do if we had the opportunity to invest in protecting and restoring WA's natural environment? Firstly, we would listen to the 95% of Australians who say that they want more money spent on nature; we would listen to the scientists and environment groups, who set out where urgent action is needed; we would listen to First Nations people, who have 65,000 years of expertise in caring for country across this state; we would take note of the national state of the environment reports and of the assessments done by the Office of the Auditor General in WA; and we would then take the necessary steps. That would mean that two major streams of work would be properly resourced—firstly, on-ground nature conservation and restoration, and, secondly, environmental regulation, where we would have a watchdog making sure that assessments and licence conditions were, firstly, appropriately set and, secondly, not being breached.

In the first category, I will give a list of the on-ground nature conservation and restoration work that we would undertake. We would start by ensuring that every threatened species and ecological community had a recovery plan in place and we would ensure that those recovery plans were properly implemented and enforced. These are in no particular order. We would also fully fund landcare across the state, which would involve providing resources to the incredible people who work in their communities to protect and link up remnant vegetation, combat salinity, restore wetlands and riparian systems and all the work in between. These are some of the best people in the state. They work on a shoestring budget day in and day out. We would ensure that they had the funding they needed to sustain and expand their work, because we recognise the huge value that would bring to the whole of WA. We would create and fund national parks in collaboration with traditional owners, providing for the most environmentally and culturally precious places in WA to be looked after, as they have been for the last 65,000 years, for another 65,000 years and beyond. We would focus on water by protecting rivers and streams and improving water quality. We would fund the various Aboriginal community–controlled organisations that employ rangers and we would resource them to do their work in caring for country. We would stop starting megafires and calling it controlled burning, and we would use the funds—the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions has allocated $68 million for prescribed burning this year—to ensure that our rapid detection and rapid suppression technology is state of the art. We would also fund careful, discrete fires where they are needed under a strategic zoning approach, which has always been recommended by the scientists and, of course, with thousands of years of First Nations fire practice in the design and operations. Finally in this category, recognising that 90% of the original vegetation in the South West global biodiversity hotspot has already been cleared or severely degraded, we would stop any clearing of remnant and critical habitats. There is plenty of cleared land where destructive industries could be positioned. We would also drastically increase the scale and speed of restoration projects.

parts: All that happened in this particular instance was that a justice agreed to the application to allow the person out on bail for the duration of the trial because the Department of Justice—in particular, Corrective Services—had refused to provide this individual with his medication that he had previously been receiving in prison. He had been receiving medication for a period of time. That medication stopped. In the lead-up to the trial, he said that he needed the medication again. I think it was some form of anti-anxiety medication. If members are really interested in the type of medication, they can go and look it up. The department of corrective services said, "No, we're not going to give you this." The judge handling this matter then has this dilemma that if he allows this matter to go on, there will be a miscarriage of justice because the individual is not going to be fit to provide instructions on this matter. He then releases this individual—albeit supervised, as you can imagine under the circumstances—into the public. Why? It was so that the individual can go and access this medication from a private practitioner. This was not somebody asking for some illicit substance. It was a prescribed drug. Corrective Services said, "No, we're not going to give it to you."

The judge evidently felt that he was left with no option other than to release the person on bail, albeit supervised. Why should somebody like Mr Whitby be concerned about this? More to the point, why should Mr Papalia be concerned about it? They should be concerned because it resulted in a massive police operation. The police helicopter had to be used to surveil this particular individual. This was over a small, little drug that needed to be provided to this individual. It was presumably prescribed by an ethical medical practitioner, but Corrective Services said, "No, we're not going to give this to you", and as a result there was a massive police operation. We asked the government, and in particular Mr Whitby, who clearly was not very happy with the whole situation, how much this massive operation cost. Mr Whitby refused to tell Parliament. Mr Whitby is currently being investigated by the Auditor General because of a section 82 notice. We look forward in due course to the outcome of that section 82 notice investigation by the Auditor General. She will give her opinion as to whether it was reasonable and appropriate for Mr Whitby to do that.

Let us just park to one side the cost, not that it is an insignificant matter; these are taxpayers' resources. Remember, police do not have time anymore to do court security in Western Australia. The Western Australia Police Force had to tell the Department of Justice that it is not providing security in the courts anymore because it is too busy. Well, no wonder police are busy when they had to supervise Mr Pye because Corrective Services would not give him his medication. If not anyone else, it should be of concern to the Minister for Corrective Services, Mr Papalia. It is on his watch. It was his department not providing this medication to this accused person that resulted in this truly extraordinary sequence of events.

parts: The government's response, of course, was to pull the bill for a year. It just pulled the bill. It disappeared beneath the waves. We continued to raise it. I have an observation on the budget and the announcement. I can only think that it is a good landing the government has made here, but jeez, couldn't that $40 million have been used last year when we raised these concerns; when the defects were revealed; when the state of the building condition assessment was revealed?

I turn to our teaching workforce in the brief time I have left. heading: Local government
subject: Local government
parts: As has already been mentioned, local governments oversee close to $50 billion in community assets, support the majority of public roads and account for $44.5 billion in annual expenditure. My electorate of Murray–Wellington has about 1,700 kilometres of local roads, so keeping those roads in good condition needs focus from not only an asset management point of view, but it also needs funding from the state and federal governments, which unfortunately has not been forthcoming. It has been declining over the years. It is becoming more and more difficult for local governments to provide services and support, and keep the assets that they need. We have to remember that they are the frontline for emergency management, they are the custodians of much of our community infrastructure and they are increasingly the safety net for failing government services, which is part of this motion. Under the Cook government, financial regulatory pressures have been placed on them and they are feeling at breaking point. Many of them feel they are not heard and do not feel the love coming from this government.

Just consider the information in the Auditor General's Financial Audit Results Local Government 2025, when it sounded the alarm. It highlighted that the financial sustainability of local governments is under severe pressure due to operating losses, declining cash reserves and the increasing burden of state compliance and complexity. They were the Auditor General's comments. The sector's ability to meet its short-term obligations is in steady decline, and why? It is because the state government is systematically cost shifting more and more of its core responsibilities onto the shoulders of local governments and that means the shoulders of local ratepayers. When local governments have more to do, they do not have many options. The only option is to get grants or to put up rates. We all know how unpopular local governments are when they put up rates, but this government tends to put more responsibility on them and then they bear the responsibility of telling the bad news to their local ratepayers.

Take primary health care in some local governments. Due to the systematic failures of the state government to provide adequate rural and remote health care, some local councils are being forced to divert their own funds just to keep medical doctors' doors open. That should not be happening in Western Australia. It seems to be happening more and more. Cost shifting is occurring not only in health care. If we look at the recent budget, we will see that the government allocated only $4.8 million to manage the shot-hole borer. It completely ignores the Western Australian Local Government Association's advice that it will cost about $45 million over four years to stop the spread. It always seems to be like "Here's a few dollars; the rest over to you, local government." Local governments are loaded with more and more responsibilities. I know that some members have been in local government; many have come through that path. I will be interested to hear their comments when they say that the government is doing everything for local governments and they should not complain. It would not be true, would it? We know that they are doing it tough in so many areas.

heading: Estimates of revenue and expenditure
subject: Estimates of revenue and expenditure
parts: I want to talk about some of the comments the Treasurer made following the budget. There has been an interesting flavour to the past week and a half. One of the things I want to say—I mentioned this in a speech last week—is that I believe the way in which this Treasurer approaches her role is undermining confidence in the government because it undermines credibility in the Treasurer herself. A Treasurer's ability to do their job effectively relies, in part, on whether people trust what they say. They want to trust that the numbers are honest. They want to trust that the projections in the budget are credible. They want to trust that they, the members of the public, have been told the full story. Increasingly, Western Australians are beginning to question whether the Treasurer is being up-front with them. We have seen this repeatedly. We have seen it in the way the Treasurer talks about debt.

I mentioned a speech last week; the spokesman for the Treasurer was just cherrypicking forecasts to try to say what debt was under the previous government. We have audited financial reports that say what it was and that were handed down six, seven or eight years ago with the Auditor General's stamp of approval. We do not need to go back 10 years and pick some random forecasts based on overly pessimistic and ultimately wrong assumptions from Treasury officials. That is not an honest way to present numbers. That is misleading. It may be politically advantageous, but it is misleading. It undercuts the credibility of the Treasurer when she and the people who work for her, represent her and provide her comments to the press do things like that.

The Labor government and this Treasurer like to present themselves as the sole guardians of fiscal responsibility while conveniently ignoring the enormous revenue windfalls they have received. The reality is that this government has received unprecedented revenue growth and still managed to substantially increase net debt. That matters because Western Australians understand the difference between managing money well and getting lucky. Secondly, we see it again in the government's claims about infrastructure funding from Canberra. I have had a fair bit to say in this place about infrastructure funding from Canberra. Despite the overall outcome still being bad, last night I was pleased to see Western Australia's infrastructure funding, combined with GST payments, improving in the federal budget. It is hard for it not to improve when our GST share will go from 75c to 82c. The government would have to significantly cut infrastructure payments to get that number back to the trajectory it was on previously.

There is also the Road Trauma Trust Account. It is not my portfolio area; it is Hon Julie Freeman's and she is away on urgent parliamentary business. I think I am a little bit more satisfied that expenditure out of that account has approximated something more proper, orderly and consistent with its original design purpose, as has recently been the case under this government. Funds were improperly used on projects that were not appropriately specced and not properly evaluated. The Office of the Auditor General quite properly focused on that area of criticism a number of years ago. I have not seen the full outcome of governance improvements in that particular area, but I am pleased that money now seems to be freed up for the designed purpose.

One of the more curious inclusions in this list, however, is something called the Resources Community Investment Initiative project. This was trumpeted in November 2022 under then Premier Hon Mark McGowan. Again, it was another front-page splash. It was a political scheme to harness the rivers of money emanating from the iron ore boom for particular projects. The concept was they would raise this fund to a billion dollars and the government would make such-and-such contribution. Some very large and notable respected resources companies all pledged a commitment to do this, but it seemed to be just cobbled together on the fly. Now, after three years of operation, the closing balance is $20 million, which is a long way short of the billion that was speculated at the time of the release. Perhaps it is an area of focus or attention that the government has not had as much love or support for in recent times. I think it was more properly the brainchild of Hon Mark McGowan. heading: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
subject: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
parts: I thank the member for Murray–Wellington for his constructive contribution to the debate and for the opposition's support for this bill. I want to turn briefly to a number of matters the member raised. Hopefully, my explanation means a very detailed consideration in detail will not be necessary because some of my comments now might answer some of the questions that he raised.

The member referred to concerns raised by the Auditor General about the administration of statutory declarations in her 2022 performance audit. While the three agencies audited—the former Department of Finance, Main Roads and Western Power—have since made improvements, this government recognises that reliance on statutory declarations from head contractors alone falls short of providing the level of compliance insurance required. Statutory declarations embedded in contractual arrangements do not necessarily provide a contract principal with a clear or timely basis to withhold payment from a head contractor that is not meeting its payment obligations or duties. A false statutory declaration may attract criminal consequences, but it does not of itself remedy the misapplication of funds intended for subcontractors. The bill we are debating directly addresses those shortcomings through the introduction of a head claim statement process and by providing clearer and more effective powers to withhold payment when requirements are not met. This ensures that state agencies and government trading enterprises have the necessary authority to take decisive, timely and meaningful action when requirements are not met.

I agree with the member's observation that withholding payments from a head contractor, even when errors may be minor, can have significant impacts on the business and on other broader contracting chains. In practice, it is anticipated that agencies and their contract superintendents and administrators will rarely need to exercise this power. The existence of a clear withholding mechanism is expected to be sufficient to address noncompliance; however, the current contractual framework for project bank accounts does not provide this effective enforcement lever.

The member for Murray–Wellington also raised the issue of the oversight of payments made by state agencies to head contractors. Given the volume of transactions on state government projects, it is neither practical nor proportionate for agencies to monitor all downstream payments to subcontractors in real time. Such an approach would materially impede project delivery and require significant resourcing, which would not represent an efficient use of public funds. Under existing project bank account arrangements, agencies undertake targeted assurance activities, including spot checks, and there are established avenues for subcontractors to raise concerns, including through the Small Business Commissioner, with options for confidential and anonymous reporting. In addition, agencies maintain reporting mechanisms. For example, the Department of Housing and Works provides a dedicated industry liaison service for reporting nonpayment or other concerns.

The Auditor General recommended audited entities tighten and refine their mechanisms, and, where necessary, each committed to do so and implemented them. The expectation is that many of those arrangements will continue for projects subject to a construction trust. In addition, the bill introduces further protections, including expanded rights for subcontractor beneficiaries to suspend works when required payments have not been made into a trust account, and to inspect and copy relevant accounting records. Failure by a head contractor trustee to comply with such a request constitutes a breach of fiduciary duty and may attract a penalty of up to $50,000.

In relation to the member's question on proposed section 76O, which is inserted by clause 22 of this bill, the provision requires a head contractor trustee to address any shortfall in a construction trust account when on the day a construction payment is received under the trust contract, there are insufficient funds to meet amounts due and owing to some contractor beneficiaries. I think that is a really important measure. Importantly, the obligation arises when a construction payment has in fact been made into the account. When a construction payment by the state principal under the trust contract is delayed for some reason, proposed section 76O is not engaged, although contractual obligations to pay subcontractors may still apply. When a partial construction payment is made due to a dispute with the state principal, it is the obligation of a head contractor or trustee to cover any resulting shortfall in amounts due and owing to the subcontractor beneficiary likely to arise. In these circumstances, it is appropriate that the head contractor or trustee pursues its claim against the state principal while ensuring subcontractor beneficiaries are paid amounts properly due and owing under the subcontract. Subcontractors not being party to the trust contract, and therefore lacking the necessary privity of contract, are otherwise unable to enforce any claim under the trust contract and would be at a disproportionate financial risk if forced to wait for the resolution of a claim by the head contractor.

heading: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
subject: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
parts: I talked a bit earlier about the question around having 28 days to make a repayment, and it is worth unpacking that a little bit further. Again, it is almost laughable, but we were told in the briefing that the original timeframe was 14 days. I mean, I do not know what was going on when people were drafting this. They got their feedback from the Western Australian Local Government Association and they generously chose to extend that 14 days out to 28. As I said, they are both ridiculous. Frankly, it is just setting up local governments to fail. Again, that is unnecessary. I note there is an amendment around this on the supplementary notice paper that we will also be supporting, but it is worth reading out what WALGA has told us on this matter. It stated:

The requirement to process and issue refunds within 28 days is unreasonable and administratively unworkable. Local Governments need sufficient time to identify affected ratepayers, source funds, and obtain appropriate approvals that meet their statutory obligations under the Local Government Act 1995 and guidelines from the Officer of the Auditor General for budget amendments on borrowings.

That is the end of that quote. I know my criticisms of the 28 days were quite strong; can I just say that they are completely backed up by the sector. I would be fascinated to hear the minister explain to us why 28 days made it into this legislation, and in what world that is acceptable.

heading: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
subject: Building and Construction Industry (Security of Payment) Amendment Bill 2026
parts: The third point it raised was that the scheme needed real penalties. The report said that the Building Services Board needed real teeth to penalise bad behaviour, including issuing demerit points and excluding individuals with a history of insolvency from having and holding a building registration. The report said fairer contracts are needed. They need a statutory right to progress payments that override unfair contracts. The report mandated written contracts for jobs over $20,000 and a ban on unreasonable time bars and clauses that restrict a subbie's rights to claim payment. The report was explicit. It identified the problems. It is not that the problem existed; it was more what was needed to be done.

The Auditor General's 2022 finding was particularly damning. It said there was a total lack of due diligence and that state government entities completely failed to implement effective controls to protect subcontractor payments, leaving the most vulnerable exposed. It also said that blindly accepting flawed paperwork was endemic. Departments routinely accepted statutory declarations without due scepticism and approved forms that were unsigned, predated or lacked declarations of truth. The Auditor General also said that the government relies almost entirely on subcontractors complaining to identify issues, which completely fails because many of the subbies, as we know, were terrified of commercial retribution and losing future work. The Auditor General also identified that there was zero proactive oversight. The report said there was a total absence of whole-of-government leadership on payment protections, and agencies routinely failed to conduct proactive spot checks to verify head contractors are actually paying their bills.

When we asked questions about why the bill exists and why it is here today, it was pretty clear that it was because what we have is not working well enough. We also know that subcontractors are staying exposed because the protections on paper were not being administered with the discipline that people would expect. The government itself has now concluded that the existing public bank account framework is too cumbersome to keep going with; 100 pages of documents are too cumbersome.

I think about where the opposition has some questions and comments. We really know that changing the mechanism is only half the job. The harder question is whether the government—all governments—has learned from past failures that made this bill necessary. As I said earlier, implementation is going to be the real test.

The Auditor General's findings were not primarily about legal form; they were about the administration and statutory declarations that were incomplete or plainly wrong being waived through the system. Agencies were leaning on complaints to surface problems, even though subcontractors said openly that they were frightened to complain. Practical tools to address poor payment behaviour were thin on the ground. Basic verification before money was released was not often happening, and if the failures of the previous system were administrative, just changing the architecture under this bill will not fix that on its own. A claim statement is only useful if it has been read, and withholding power is only meaningful if somebody is willing to use it. A trust account is only protective if compliance is continuing to be monitored. In the end, a complaints process is only real if subcontractors trust it enough to pick up the phone and make a complaint. The scope is limited in power.

The trust scheme covers the principal to the head contractor and the head contractor to the first-tier subcontractor, so it does not go down through the chain. There are reasons for that, of course. It only has the same scope as the current legislation through the project bank accounts, and it does not reach down all through that chain. We know that there are many layers in the contracting system. It does not extend, of course, in this case to the private sector, so one could argue that there is a two-tiered system: one for government contracts and one for private sector contracts. In its introduction, the government said that it will see how it goes with the public sector first, but there are reasonable arguments that this sort of fairness needs to be in the private sector as well. The state, through this bill, can use its procurement leverage first. Not loading a full trust model onto smaller operators down the chain that would struggle with the compliance burden is fine, of course, but this is targeted reform, and I just wanted to make the point that it is not a universal fix for all subcontractors across the board.

Proposed section 76O of the bill, the shortfall rule, needs close scrutiny as well. This provision says that if there is not enough money in the trust account to pay a subcontractor when payment falls due, the trustee must immediately top it up. That has a cash flow implication for the subcontractor or the lead contractor. If there is any hold-up in that payment, obviously, there will be concerns about cash flow issues for them as well. Although the logic of getting the subcontractor paid is clear, if the head contractor is short, they will have to top it up themselves. Those cash flows can have significant implications, particularly for large contract projects that have large sums involved. It means that if a government agency drags its feet or disputes part of a claim, the head contractor may be forced to finance the dispute out of its own working capital. That may be defensible in some cases, but obviously in others there may be due reason and that is not fair. Either way, the government needs to be very clear about how this practice works, and we will talk about that in consideration in detail. Some clarification is required there, especially for head contractors running on tight margins. This is not an argument against protecting subcontractors but an argument for watching where the risk actually falls and lands.

The Auditor General already explained why complaint-driven oversight does not always work. Subcontractors will still fear being blackballed. A control system that relies on the most vulnerable people in the chain putting their hands up without proper protection is not a good control system alone. It is a way of recording problems after the damage has already been done. If this new regime falls back on that approach, I am afraid that the same failures will follow, so we have to continue to scrutinise and watch that.

We need implementation tests, not just checklists. The government will be measured against a clear set of tests. Will the agencies be trained properly and in time? Will the Department of Treasury and Finance step up and provide genuine whole-of-government leadership this time, or will each agency be left to fend for itself again? Will claim statements be checked, with proactive auditing and spot-checks, or will it stay reactive, waiting for somebody to complain? We have explained the issues with that. Will subcontractors finally have a complaints pathway that they are not afraid to use? I think that is the key question. There is a real question about retaliation in the sector. Will any shortfall be monitored so it does not crush otherwise viable head contractors? Will this rollout be staged appropriately and properly? A rushed implementation would be worse than no reform at all because it would discredit the whole model, which we believe is worth supporting.

We need to make sure that subcontractors' voices are heard. I believe that a direct survey of the people the bill is meant to protect should be part of the implementation and checking processes. It should be anonymous, independent and industry wide. Are they actually being paid on time? Do they trust the system that we are implementing, and do they feel safe using the complaint pathway that is in the legislation? Are they being asked to sign off on payments they have not received, which was the very practice that the old statutory declaration regime allowed? If the bill is meant to help, it has to be trustworthy and we have to make sure that those who it is meant to protect have a voice.

The fourth point is a need for independent oversight. This should not be an agency itself. I propose that it should be the Auditor General or some other independent body, with access to records, claim statements, trust accounts and contracting data. The same scrutiny that exposed the failures of the PBA system in the first place is needed to check on this new system. I believe those reports should be tabled openly and transparently, perhaps in this Parliament, so that we can see the evidence, question it and hold ourselves and the government to account. Of all that, if we get the feedback, we need to be willing to adjust and to be flexible, to tighten the rules and to strengthen withholding provisions, and to improve protections and our own methodology of implementation.

In closing, the opposition has approached this bill in a constructive way. We are supportive of any genuine improvements, and we are certainly willing to back sensible change and reform. Let us also be clear-eyed about the failures that made the reform necessary in the first place. We should not confuse tidier statutes with the problem being solved. The industry has told us the issues, and, as I said at the beginning, we need to make sure that we address the real concerns of those subcontractors and listen to their voices. The opposition supports the bill and I commend my comments to the house.
