heading: Treasurer-Performance
subject: Treasurer—Performance
parts: The second point raised in this motion is (1)(b), which concerns the Help to Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill. This government is very aware that everyone in our community here in Western Australia deserves a safe and affordable place that they can call home. The government—in particular, the Treasurer—is doing everything it can to unlock residential land and build new housing supply. We introduced the Help to Buy bill in this place, and it was scrutinised and progressed. We have a unique situation here in WA. Unlike other jurisdictions, we have a dedicated Standing Committee on Uniform Legislation and Statutes Review, which means that, unlike other states and territories, we have a defined process and therefore an extended timeframe for legislation to be considered. That was also explained in Parliament by the Treasurer, and I do not think it is a fair assessment to include this part of the motion and have it reflect upon an entire year of the Treasurer's performance.

The third point, (1)(c), is around concerns about the Perth parking levy. Members will note that the Auditor General's Administration of the Perth Parking Levy report of 2022–23 identified issues around that. However, the government introduced legislation in 2023 to improve and modernise the Perth Parking Management Act 1999 and the administration of the levy. The government stated that the bill included new requirements for expenditure from the Perth parking management account to be reported in the Department of Treasury and Finance's annual report, and that it would provide more flexibility in how levy funds could actually be invested.

In 2023, the Minister for Transport also told Parliament that the issue provided an opportunity to improve the amenity and assets of the City of Perth, support more people living in the city and reform the levy to bring more benefit to the CBD, ratepayers and the community. It was a definitive response to that audit finding.

Hon Samantha Rowe : Right. I think what the opposition fails to see with that project is that governments can make investments, like the Perth entertainment and sporting precinct, and still manage the state's budget and finances, which is what we are doing. We can do both. In 2025, the Treasurer managed a budget that delivered cost-of-living support, infrastructure investment, housing measures, health investment and continued surpluses. The budget recorded $963 million in further support for WA households. We had below-inflation household fees and charges for a sixth consecutive year, a $150 power bill credit for every WA household, the rollout of battery rebates and no-interest loans, the introduction of the "Go Anywhere" fare, free public transport for school students, rent relief, KidSport and the expansion of the school breakfast program. We can have targeted relief that helps WA households and communities today and at the same time invest in projects for the future. We can do all of that and also have a really strong balance sheet, and that is what our Treasurer is doing and is able to do. We are able to walk and chew gum at the same time!

We have a really strong record, and that is not talked about in the motion put forward this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. The motion does not acknowledge our government's surpluses, the Aaa credit rating, the debt position, the jobs that have been created, the infrastructure that has been delivered or the reforms that have been progressed. None of that is talked about in this motion. One would have thought that maybe they should be, given we are looking at the Treasurer's record for 2025. The motion does not acknowledge that the government changed the law for survivors of historical child sexual abuse, that we actually progressed the Help to Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill or that we responded to the Auditor General's report findings—none of that is acknowledged in the motion.

The Treasurer's performance last year should be assessed against the responsibilities of the office, but this motion does not take any of that into account. Do we have a state with a really strong financial position? Do we have a really strong economy here in WA? Yes, we do. Has WA continued to deliver operating surpluses? Yes, we have. Has debt remained affordable? Yes, it has. Has the state retained the highest credit rating of Aaa? Yes. We have done all of those things while also continuing to invest in infrastructure, housing, health, transport and energy, but none of those are acknowledged or taken into account in this motion. I would have thought a lot of that, if not all of it, is what our Treasurer should be judged on. If we were to judge our Treasurer on that, I have to say that she would have to be one of the strongest Treasurers in the country. Over consecutive years, she has been able to deliver surpluses for this state and make sure that we keep the Aaa credit rating, while continuing to invest in so many different areas that have real impacts for Western Australians. I would have thought that means our Treasurer is actually doing an outstanding job here in WA, and I am really proud of the work that she and our government have done and what has been achieved already in this state. Tomorrow, we will have the opportunity to see another budget by this Treasurer, and, again, I am really confident that investments will make sure that Western Australians are not only looked after today but also set up for the future. That is what governments have to do. I do not accept the points raised in this motion as being a fair assessment of the Treasurer's record for 2025. I absolutely do not. I think any Treasurer around Australia would look at WA and think that we are in a very, very strong position.

heading: Joint Standing Committee on the Commissioner for Children and Young People
subject: Joint Standing Committee on the Commissioner for Children and Young People
parts: Hon Nick Goiran : This, Review Report 2025: The work of the Commissioner for Children and Young People 2024–25, is report 2 of the Joint Standing Committee on the Commissioner for Children and Young People. The committee has assessed and analysed the work of the commissioner in the last financial year. I draw to members' attention that there is, if you like, a structural issue that is worth members of the committee and government considering; that is, the tenure of the Commissioner for Children and Young People.

Under the arrangement that exists in Western Australia, a commissioner is appointed for, if I recall correctly, a period of five years and is capable of reappointment for a further five years. That is the limit. A person can be the commissioner for a maximum of 10 years—five years plus five years. I have been looking with interest at what other jurisdictions do. It is worth noting that some jurisdictions have a superior model whereby a person is appointed for a fixed term with no possibility of reappointment. I think historically this committee has looked at some of those tenures, including that in the United Kingdom, which may have a tenure of seven or eight years and then that is it. By way of comparison, here in Western Australia, the Auditor General, who is also a parliamentary officer who reports to Parliament, has a single term of 10 years after which time they cannot be reappointed. As it has been put to me over the years, the benefit of such a model is that it ensures that there is no structural deficiency that might, presumably, unintentionally but also subconsciously impact the strength of the voice of the Commissioner for Children and Young People. In other words, they do not feel at any stage that their voice needs to be less strong, because if it is too strong, the government of the day might not reappoint them. For example, the situation in Scotland—if I recall correctly—is that the entire process is managed by the Scottish Parliament. I think our jurisdiction is reasonably unique in that we have a standalone committee that has responsibility for overseeing the work of the Commissioner for Children and Young People and even though we have all of those parliamentary links and the person is supposed to be—and, I think, is—independent of government, it is still executive government that makes the appointment. Executive government decides who will be the Commissioner for Children and Young People, as I believe is the case in England. But then they also have the power to decide whether or not the person is reappointed. Under the Scottish model, it is entirely run by the Parliament. As I understand it, the Scottish Parliament—members of the committee may want to look at this—even sets the budget for its Commissioner for Children and Young People. It seems to me that this is something worth looking at in terms of the structure of our model. All my comments this afternoon have no reflection whatsoever on either the current Commissioner for Children and Young People or her predecessors. I simply want to identify that work could be done by the standing committee—in addition to the excellent work it is already doing—whether in this calendar year or otherwise, to look at whether there is an opportunity for us to do something different. I must say that I have some sympathy for the case that we should have a single term, perhaps longer than five years, as is the current case. What exactly should that be? I am sure fair minds will disagree on that. Some might say six, seven or eight years. I do not think too much turns on that. It might be eight years simply because that reflects two terms of Parliament, but that might not be helpful. Those are the kinds of things that the joint standing committee can reflect on and potentially make recommendations to the government.

In summary, I think there is a benefit of not only a single term, but also this other aspect of who ultimately controls the budget of the Commissioner for Children and Young People. Is it a truly independent position appointed by executive government with the purse strings controlled by government, as is the case as I understand it in England, or should it be done as it is done in the Scottish Parliament where there is total control by Parliament? Perhaps there could be a hybrid model between all those things? They are all things for the committee to look at.

heading: Cook government-Home ownership
subject: Cook government—Home ownership
parts: We know it is often more expensive to build in regional areas than it is in the city, and that is another barrier to the people in regional areas getting their housing shortages taken care of. We know that in many areas in regional Western Australia housing is very, very expensive. In the North West, rents are well over $1,000 and sometimes $2,000 a week. I was up in Port Hedland a couple of weeks ago, and we looked at some of the rentals that are available. Rent was up to $2,500 per week for a fairly modest house. These are extraordinary amounts of money for a basic house in a town that is desperately short of housing, not just because of the cost to build the houses, but because of a lack of direction from government over many years to provide all the infrastructure and all the necessary prerequisites for that land to be developed. We know of the situation earlier in this term of government where a development was knocked back—I think it was 87 units from memory—because there was not enough water to provide for it. Now, suddenly, the water has been found. But that just goes to show that there is a cavalier disregard for the needs of Western Australia's regions by this government.

If we look at some of the public housing, we see 45,000 social homes in Western Australia, a waitlist of 23,237 applications and 8,023 on the priority list. The waitlist has increased by 56% since 2019. It is not getting better; it is getting worse. It is getting a lot worse. We know that this government has a problem accepting the fact that it needs to do something about its maintenance regimes to improve the waitlist. The Auditor General's Management of Housing Maintenance Information report was tabled in August 2025, showing that of the 240,000 maintenance jobs it looked at, 85% are reactive, which means that they are costly. They are not actually getting out there, getting the job done or getting a program to make it all work. Instead, they are relying on reactive results. I also know from talking to some of my constituents who rely on the contractors to come and take care of maintenance issues that they can wait a very, very long time indeed for someone to come and do that. I have heard stories of people who have a problem with the plumbing in their house. A plumber comes out from Geraldton to Meekatharra, visits and does a bit of work but does not address any of the other issues that might exist in the house because that is not what is on the work order and goes back home again, leaving the job half done. These are the types of inefficiencies that we are seeing this government allow to continue.

I would very much like to know where the renewal of the head contract is for the areas of Meekatharra, the Mid West, Gascoyne and the Pilbara—I think the Great Southern and South West are all under programs—which is a $158 million contract. Where is that renewal and what is being done to improve some of the efficiencies of that group? Some of the stories I have heard would make members shake their heads.

heading: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
subject: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
parts: A $1.6 billion residual outside the named items in the Treasurer's advance and a government that runs a budget speech with no discrete line item for the policy areas in this chamber—that is most actively pressing—indicates a government that has structurally limited the scrutiny territory that we possess and have available to us but is not being utilised in this house. Now, I am not saying it is intentional; I say it is the effect. No aspersions are being cast. This is simply what we are facing. But the effect is what concerns me, because the effect is, in my particular case, a Parliament that is being asked to authorise a spend it cannot interrogate on policy areas it cannot debate. This is a fundamental attack on the ability of this house to exert control over how we spend the valuable tax moneys that we are then perhaps giving out. One of the contentions I will look at in the future is how much of the money that we have as a resource given to us is being wasted, squirrelled away and lost in the inevitable trickle down into the sewers, if you like, or where the moneys are being wasted. I can give numerous examples, as anyone who has worked in government can attest.

In the other place, the member for Central Wheatbelt drew attention to the Auditor General Amendment Bill 2022, which was passed by both houses but has not yet received royal assent four years on. I am not going to go back into that bill and I do not propose to do more than note what its non-assented status communicates. It communicates that this Parliament's principal scrutiny officer is operating in a state of legislative ambiguity that has been allowed to persist. That is a comment I make. The Treasurer's advance authorisation of this scale with an Auditor General amendment bill that has been left in suspension and a budget structure that omits discrete lines of active policy debate, taken together, describes a scrutiny environment that is markedly—how can I put this?—weaker than the one this chamber would like to have inherited. That is simply a pattern I think I am seeing.

An area I would also like to mention was created by the then Premier, Hon Mark McGowan, in 2017—the debt reduction account, which was a 2017 election commitment, I believe. It held, as planned at the end of the year, the balance of zero, because the purpose of that is to pay off the debt. If we look at this, we are understanding that at the moment, the current total debt, as far as I can calculate, and that is not an easy calculation, is about $1 billion more than the case in 2021. I mentioned earlier the 625 years that an ordinary person would be required to work to earn that amount of money. In that time, the debt reduction account has paid off around about $3.5 billion, so $4.5 billion of debt increased in the time when we have had a fiscal bounty in the state as well. It begs the question: How have we actually been managing our finances? Are they as fiscally appropriate as one would wish? The answer, I think, is probably not. With the forces mentioned earlier, had we been in a time of straitened circumstances or a recession, would we have had to act differently? I think the answer is: yes, we would have. But I am a simple doctor. What do I know?

heading: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
subject: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
parts: … The Government Financial Responsibility Act 2000 requires the release of audited whole-of-government financial results, consistent with external reporting requirements, within 90 days of the financial year-end.

This document also contains the opinion of the Auditor General to give a bit of extra flavour of the level of scrutiny that exists on these numbers. This is not a forecast that a spokesman for the Treasurer cherrypicked from some budget from 11 years ago or something; this is a document that existed after that financial year is done. It has the opinion of the Auditor General, commenting on the credibility of the numbers in it. I can simply do what that spokesman for the Treasurer could have done but did not do because it was not politically convenient and read the net debt figure for 2016–17. This is table 1, "Key Budget Aggregates". The total public sector net debt on 30 June 2016–17 was $31.964 million. That is what it says. That is not a forecast; it is an actual. It was audited and tabled in September, months after the financial year ended. When that particular spokesman for this particular Treasurer had the choice of using this number or using a forecast that was long redundant and based on forecasts that ended up being wrong, the spokesman chose the forecast figure and the figure based on Treasury assumptions that were incorrect.

Again, those three examples are of using the wrong net debt figure in December when speaking to the media and doing the midyear budget update, using an undiscounted number to describe the economic return on the Perth Park racetrack, which substantially exaggerated the economic benefits of the project, and not answering basic questions about infrastructure funding from the opposition, particularly in the context of the fight for our fair share of GST. If we cannot even get answers like that and instead get these colourful responses that focus on three projects, I think that says a lot about the approach of this particular Treasurer and this particular Labor government towards budgets, transparency, expenditure and, frankly, respect for the processes of the Parliament. It is completely legitimate for opposition and crossbenchers to scrutinise these things. It is completely legitimate for these questions to be asked, and the Treasurer should answer those questions. Sometimes questions are not politically convenient. I understand that Treasurers sometimes play politics, and sometimes oppositions play politics, but there is a point where, in avoiding something that is politically inconvenient, the credibility of the person engaging in that behaviour is undercut. I have just given three examples of when this Treasurer did not meet the standards that previous Treasurers of different persuasions in this state have met. That is very disappointing and does not bode well for what we are going to see this week in the forward estimates or what is in this bill that I am speaking on. It is a grim time for many Western Australians who are really struggling right now but listening to a government make announcement after announcement telling them just how good things are and, according to them, how well they have apparently handled things.

This government does make choices. It is not completely a victim of global circumstances or the like. Many of the outcomes we are experiencing reflect choices. I would say that this reflects the fear that I hear from constituents and members of my community who I deal with day to day. The choices that this government has made have not delivered where it matters most right now. Big spending has not made people in this state better off. In many cases, it has contributed to inflation, which is simply adding to the cost of living for everyone. Our state is wealthier, and the government can throw around lots of big macro figures, but the residents who we represent are not feeling it. They feel worse off. They do not feel like they are part of Team WA or that these outcomes are fair for them. They feel like they are paying the cost for poor decisions elsewhere. That is the disconnect we see right now between the state government and many members of the community. We are the wealthiest state in the nation. In the wealthiest state of the nation, I think it is fair to say that Western Australians should be getting ahead. They should be feeling the benefits of that prosperity. I think Western Australians deserve that.

They have worked hard and been responsible. They have done what their parents and grandparents did in tough times, but under this government, in this economy, with demand being boosted artificially by excessive spending, as is reflected in this bill today, that is not working like it used to. It is not working as it did for previous generations, and they are struggling. I think that they deserve better than that. They deserve a government that manages money responsibly, as they are expected to do. They deserve a government that is focused on the fundamentals and not distracted by pet projects or by playing silly politics during budget estimates, when they did not answer questions about spending and did not include inflation in a 30-year forecast, and they continually used discredited numbers of net debt from 10 years ago, when we have audited accounts signed off and endorsed by an opinion from the Auditor General that was tabled in Parliament and could be referred to. I think that people are sick of it. They are sick of the politics and the political games from this Treasurer. They just want a Treasurer and a government that are focused on getting the basics right and saying things that go to the heart of the issues they face. They are not getting that. As I said, I think that the Reserve Bank of Australia is reflecting that lack of confidence as well. Western Australians deserve a government that ensures the benefits of living in the wealthiest state in the nation are felt by the people who live here.

I will conclude by saying that we support this bill because we, as an opposition, want to be responsible. We understand that it is not good for the state or the Treasurer to run out of money, but I have said several things in this speech that the government should take note of. There is a disconnect between voters and what this government is doing and saying, and there is a disconnect between the expectations of households, as Hon Julie Freeman referred to several times in her speech, and what this government is doing. It raises serious questions about the choices this government is making and whether it is truly focused on the impacts facing people out there. I will reiterate that we will support the passage of this bill, but it was important to raise the concerns that I raised.

heading: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
subject: Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill 2026
parts: People have a budget to build a house. They have a pretty good idea of what that is. It is their money so they are very concerned about what that money will do and how that money will work for them, yet it seems when we come into this magical place, the idea of money having real value seems to go out the window. We throw numbers like $1.2 billion and $800 million around as if they are nothing. When you travel particularly into the regions, but even out to the eastern suburbs where I spend much of my time, those numbers really mean something. I was out in the Goldfields last week and there are shires out there that for years have been funding their own doctors and their own health services because they are not being funded by the state. We start throwing those figures around and say, "It's going to cost us another $50 million for this particular issue" with a metropolitan police station or something that is happening here because it is gold-plated or because it is blowing out in time. Shires are raising $1 million a year to put a doctor in place so they can give him or her a place to live and a car and all those sort of things. These figures really mean something. When local governments have a small rates base, those people are paying. Every time those rates go up, it hurts. I just get really frustrated with this Monopoly money kind of mentality.

I had not intended to go into this ICT thing; it is IT communications and technology. I will just go back to last year when there was the Auditor General's review, the 2025 Transparency Report — Major IT Projects. It was interesting what the Auditor General said. She talked about all these IT projects that I think are roughly $1 billion over cost, and many of them had run way over schedule. She said:

… half of the projects have had their estimated cost at least doubled. While Government may choose not to fully fund project estimates at the outset, they are key to informing investment advice and decisions and as such should be as robust as possible.

The other part of this is within the project world. Every project is assessed on the basis of risk and, depending on that risk level, the project manager will decide on a contingency component. High-risk projects have a higher contingency; lower risk projects usually have a lower contingency. Usually, if the cost projections are tight and historically reliable in terms of the metrics and tools that have been used, the contingency is based upon that. There are some big projects within the project world that are similar to the size of this request here. Some of those projects are worth well over $1 billion. A project's contingency is usually set at the outset. If a project manager wanted to change the contingency of a project, it would require a huge amount of information and justification that the risk has significantly changed, therefore they need to negotiate another contingency. It is actually extremely rare that that would happen. We have this very vague, "Well, there could be a natural disaster or something, or there could be some expenses come up", yet the government is asking for a provision for another $1.2 billion on top of the $1.2 billion that was already there. The government is asking for contingency upon contingency. I can tell members, as someone who has put variations to clients, if one just chucks a contingency on a variation, one is usually going to get smacked back. The client will see through it and will query that. The government needs to be able to provide a justification, and we did not really see any of that in the explanatory memorandum or in the debate.

The other part of it is that within any of these costings, when someone puts forward a project and any of these variations and contingencies, they have to have enough detail in it to know what can be measured against it and what the control is. Going back again to these ICT projects, these things were raised in the Auditor General's report, and in the conclusions and findings, the various departments said, "Yes, we will put these measures in place." I will refer particularly to the police, not because I am picking on them, but because that was the contract I was dealing with at the time. They said, "Yes, we will put measures in place to control spending." When I queried them, nothing had been put in place. It was just a general, "Yes, we have a system in place and we have a project manager in place to do that". They did not say, "We have a crisis here because we are blowing out budgets year on year." It was not even year on year; it was every few months. They did not say, "We are blowing out the budgets but we will just continue business as usual and tell you that we're managing it." I can tell members now that someone in the project world would not get away with that, and I do not think that the people of Western Australia should have to just accept that on the face of it.

We are being asked to approve this bill, which will give a $1.2 billion extension to effectively the credit card debt. If the Treasurer wants to go out and spend money, she can basically do it. It has also been raised today that the Treasurer's Advance Authorisation Bill is potentially being used to bypass normal budget accountability measures. We go through the whole budget process; we are about to see that happen this week, and then we will have all the budget reply speeches coming up in the next few weeks. That is part of that accountability. The shadow Treasurer and various members will pore over each part of the budget to try to give it some scrutiny and put accountability behind it. When the government asks for a provision and effectively says, "I want an extra $1.2 billion to spend on unforeseen cash flow requirements and emerging issues", which are not defined, then it just feels a bit like the government is trying to just push this through and escape some of the scrutiny. The fact has been raised by members over the course of today, some more graciously than others and some probably more bluntly, that this has been done year on year and has become part of the process. It has become a habit that the Treasurer will continue to ask for these advances as part of a strategy to have access to funds that will not be given the same sort of scrutiny that we get through the normal budget process. It is really astonishing to me that we are being asked to pass this without the detail before us.

parts: Mr Lachlan Hunter : The government is addicted to secrecy, Leader of the Opposition. We know that this government is addicted to secrecy.

I want to highlight what the Leader of the Opposition said over the weekend about the member for Landsdale making a mockery of him on ABC radio. The government is spending money that is not the government's money, so how about doing the decent thing and being up-front with the people of Western Australia and telling them how much they will cost. I will go through the list. Will it be spent on the defunded Wheatbelt Secondary Freight Network? That is a great collaboration between the state, local and Commonwealth governments. heading: Cook government-Regions-Performance
subject: Cook government—Regions—Performance
parts: The consequences are being felt across regional WA. Take ambulance ramping. In March 2017, when this government came to office, the record ambulance ramping across regional hospitals was just 6.2 hours for March 2017. Compare that to last month when it was 180 hours for February 2026. That represents patients waiting in pain and distress to be assessed and it represents ambulances unable to respond to the next emergency because we know that in regional Western Australia there is not another hospital that is easy to get to. We are seeing hospitals stretched beyond capacity. One of the main problems and challenges is bed block, which is the inability to move patients through the system because there are simply not enough beds. While we are the wealthiest state in the country, we have some of the lowest number of beds per capita. In fact, it is the second-lowest number of beds per capita in the country. Instead of building capacity—I have gone through the nine hospitals—this government has built absolutely nothing.

We are seeing services withdrawn. As the Leader of the National Party has pointed to, obstetric services have been withdrawn. In Carnarvon in the Gascoyne region, maternity services were stripped away over the last four years. The reality of this is extremely challenging for regional families. That is the reality of regional health under Labor. Let me turn to Geraldton. As the member for Geraldton knows all too well, Labor promised an upgrade of Geraldton Health Campus in 2017. It was first expected to be completed, and was promised to be completed, in 2022, yet the timeline slipped to 2024 and now the project is not expected to be completed until 2027. The Auditor General's recent transparency report confirmed what the community and the member for Geraldton knows all too well, and that is that the Geraldton Health Campus upgrade is the most delayed major project in Western Australia. It is almost five years late. That is not a planning failure; it is a failure that affects health care for the entire Mid West and speaks to this government's priorities, which are not health and certainly not regional Western Australia.

We are seeing similar issues and challenges in the South West. As the member for Warren–Blackwood knows all too well, Margaret River Hospital is already operating at capacity and struggling to meet demand. heading: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
subject: Standing Committee on Estimates and Financial Operations
parts: Budget estimates hearings are one of the most important accountability mechanisms available to this chamber. They provide a rare opportunity for members to question ministers and departments directly about government spending. Members ask questions and departments provide information and, through that process, the Western Australian public gains insight into how policy decisions are made and how taxpayer funding is being used. That is how accountability is meant to work in a Westminster system. Governments propose spending and Parliament examines the spending and, through that process, public confidence in our budget and our system of government is meant to be maintained. But this report indicates that some of that process is being undermined by the practices of ministers and ministerial officers.

One of the most significant findings concerns the failure to provide information to the committee. During the inquiry, ministers declined to provide requested information on 15 occasions. Again, this is all in the executive summary at the beginning of the report; members do not have to dig into the report to find it. In many of those cases, the explanation given was commercial confidentiality or cabinet confidentiality. There may well be circumstances in which information genuinely cannot be released. I am not disputing that, and, certainly with my previous experience working on budgets in the nation's capital, I understand some of that. But this Parliament has established and very clear safeguards to make sure that when information is refused, it is refused appropriately. A process is meant to be followed, and this committee report goes directly to that issue. Section 82 of the Financial Management Act says that when a minister refuses to provide information, that refusal must be formally reported to Parliament and the Auditor General. As I said, it is outlined in this report. That requirement exists for a reason. It exists to ensure that the decision to withhold information itself is transparent and that the Parliament, not just the committee, is aware of the refusal. It allows the refusal itself to be scrutinised. Again, this is a stock standard part of good, healthy Westminster democracy. heading: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
subject: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
parts: Resumed from 4 December 2025.

Ms Libby Mettam ( Vasse—Deputy Leader of the Opposition ) ( 1:17 :26 pm ): I rise as the lead speaker on behalf of the opposition, representing the shadow in the other place, to support the Working With Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025. This bill seeks to address a loophole in the current state-based screening system that allows individuals who are barred in another jurisdiction to obtain related work in Western Australia. This bill gives effect to the agreement by the Standing Council of Attorneys-General (SCAG) on 15 August 2025 for national mutual recognition of decisions that prohibit unsuitable people from working with children. This bill will enable information sharing about adverse working with children decisions and discussions, will recognise adverse interstate working with children decisions and will result in systematic automated checking of the national reference system to ensure that working with children card holders remain fit to work with children. It is clear that we obviously support what this bill proposes to do. I am sure many would also agree that the Auditor General undertakes and has already undertaken some important work in WA to underline the significance of this bill and what this bill represents.

Last year's Auditor General report assessed WA's progress on key actions to implement the national principles for child-safe organisations, and this is one aspect of the royal commission's recommendations. The landmark report of the five-year Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse found that major institutions across the country had failed to protect children, calling the scale of abuse in Australia a national tragedy. It made over 400 recommendations to stop this from continuing, 310 of which applied to the Western Australian Government. The audit was focused on the progress Western Australia had made on key actions to effectively implement the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, as recognised by the 2017 Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse. As I stated, we saw the Auditor General's report on this last year. I quote from the report's overview:

WA is lagging behind other jurisdictions in completing this important work. Nearly eight years after committing to doing so, WA still does not have legislation mandating compliance with the National Principles. During the audit, the State Government announced Ombudsman WA will be the oversight body. While this is welcome progress, this vital function cannot start until resourcing is confirmed and relevant legislation passed.

It has been eight years since the royal commission concluded and WA is one of two jurisdictions in the country yet to establish the necessary legislation to mandate compliance with the agreed principles on child-safe standards. While we welcome the introduction of the Ombudsman as the independent overseer of child-related work—as I have referred to already, that announcement was made during the time of the audit by the Auditor General of WA—the Ombudsman has been limited in being able to fulfil the role that was announced.

As I have stated, I am not the shadow Minister for Child Protection—that is Hon Nick Goiran in the other place—but it was noted during the briefing process that relevant organisations outside government were not consulted in relation to the development of this bill that we have here before us. Our shadow engaged with a number of stakeholders and did receive some feedback, however. The Commissioner for Children and Young People expressed support for the amendments brought forward in the bill that we have here today and in particular the requirement of the CEO to check the National Reference System, stating that continuous checking is a critical safeguard that ensures emerging risks are identified promptly and that individuals who are no longer suitable to work with children cannot continue to do so due to delays or jurisdictional gaps.

The Western Australian Local Government Association also provided a detailed submission to the government's phase 2 reform consultation paper, and its response to this bill was supportive of it creating the mechanism for cross-jurisdictional checks. WALGA raised two points that it said are not addressed by this bill—the widening of categories of persons who engage in child-related work to more appropriately reflect the variety of engagement that local government staff and members have with children, and the appointment of an independent child-safeguarding oversight body to handle complaints, as recommended by the royal commission. On this point, we note that the government did announce an oversight role, but that appointment in October last year, which is with the Ombudsman, remains unimplemented.

The Auditor General also pointed to important upgrades that are required to the legislative framework, including legislation to improve child safety as well as to address the royal commission's recommendations, including on the National Redress Scheme, the Reportable Conduct Scheme and updates to working with children checks, which we are dealing with right now. We look forward to seeing more reform to come.

I note that the communiqué of the Standing Council of Attorneys-General of November last year highlighted that WA, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory are jurisdictions that are yet to deal with legislation involving negative interstate notices. The findings of the Auditor General's report also stated:

Communities has taken a fragmented approach to leading WA's implementation of the National Principles. Since 2018, it has relied on several interagency working groups to independently identify and then complete actions … However, it did not develop an overarching implementation plan to guide its approach and steer the working groups' activities. When working groups ceased, many of their identified actions still showed as 'in progress'. As a result, Communities does not understand its current progress to support organisations to embed the National Principles or how much more needs to be done.

heading: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025
subject: Working with Children (Screening) Amendment Bill 2025

heading: Health system
subject: Health system
parts: One of the most significant pressures affecting hospital capacity sits outside the hospital system itself. That pressure is aged care. Hospitals depend on aged care functioning properly for both the people who require residential care and those who can remain at home with appropriate support services. When older Western Australians receive the support they need, health problems are identified earlier and care needs are managed sooner, and many hospital admissions can be avoided. But when those supports are not available, or when they become unaffordable, the consequences quickly flow into the hospital system. Western Australia already has fewer residential aged-care places relative to demand than the national average. The latest national data shows that there are 59.1 residential aged-care places per 1,000 older people in Western Australia, compared with 65.4 places per 1,000 nationally. At the same time, the aged-care beds we do have are more heavily occupied, with 92% occupancy in Western Australia compared with 89.9% occupancy nationally. That means when older patients finish their acute treatment in hospital and require ongoing care, there is often no aged-care support available. They are medically stable and ready for discharge, but there is nowhere safe for them to go.

On any given day in Western Australia, around 200 hospital beds are occupied by older patients who are medically ready for discharge but cannot leave because aged-care support is unavailable—either in a residential placement or with a safe return home. Doctors working in the system describe the situation as a small hospital worth of people who no longer require hospital service occupying acute beds. The problem is not just how many patients are waiting; it is how long they remain there. The WA Auditor General found that hundreds of patients waiting for aged-care services or disability services spent around 40,000 additional days in hospital after they were medically ready for discharge. That is an average of more than 80 extra days each. In other words, hospital beds are being occupied for weeks, or even months, after treatment has finished, simply because the right care is not available. Those beds represent around 3% of the state's hospital capacity. Keeping someone in a public hospital bed costs around $2,300 a day, while keeping someone in the aged-care system costs closer to $350 a day. That means the health system is spending roughly $173 million each year delivering care in hospitals that could have been provided for about $26 million by aged-care services or through home support. It is a gap of around $147 million every year. In other words, Western Australia is paying hospital prices to deliver aged-care services simply because the right care is not available at the right time. Every one of those hospital beds is a bed that cannot be used for a patient waiting in an emergency department.

There is also a growing gap in the availability and affordability of support for people living at home. Western Australia has a significantly lower rate of access to in-home care support than the national average, with only 4.7% per 1,000 people aged over 65 receiving home care support in Western Australia compared with 7.7% per 1,000 nationally. When we look at those with the most complex needs, people requiring higher level packages, we see that Western Australia fails again. Only 29% of recipients in WA receive high-level packages compared with 33.6% nationally. These packages are designed for people who have experienced significant deterioration in their health or mobility—people who may have suffered a fall, hospitalisation or had a sudden decline that means they require daily assistance. Without support at home, the risk increases quickly—falls increase, medication complications rise and hospital admissions become more likely. Once again, hospitals become the safety net.

heading: Premier's Statement
subject: Premier's Statement
parts: WA families are left waiting in limbo. Vulnerable Western Australians are now waiting significantly longer for housing than people in the rest of the country. The national median wait time for public housing is nine months. In Western Australia, the typical wait has ballooned to over 19 months and for some people, those with the greatest need, it can be over 39 months. Despite being in the greatest need category, only 15% of high-priority applicants are housed in less than three months—only 15%. Western Australia's total waitlist grew by 17.5% to 22,409 people, far exceeding the national growth rate of 12%.

We even have challenges in the maintenance of our public housing stock. The Auditor General is very clear in her latest report on the state of public housing, pointing out that the system of public housing maintenance and the information tracking system are poor and need major reform. The findings and associated commentary are quite damning, finding that 85% of maintenance is reactive, so the most costly and not meeting needs. The core conclusion is that maintenance is largely reactive rather than planned, meaning high costs and longer vacancy times. The flow-on harm is a crisis, with the pressure putting more people into homelessness. The key issue is that rents rise and supply lags, people fall into crisis and services for those in most need get stretched so that vulnerable young people are pushed into unsafe situations. The human cost of the failure to fund public housing is damning.

The government's record build is a drop in the ocean. Adding just over 1,200 homes in the last two years sounds significant until one realises that, over the same period, 2,600 additional families were added to the priority list. We are going backwards fast and are losing ground every single day. The latest report on government services further highlights a systemic failure to fund the human side of this crisis. WA's funding for frontline homelessness services remains stalled at $39.88 per person, roughly 25% below the national average of $53.15. We do not have just a building problem; it is a social services support problem.

I will talk about water. Regional Western Australians care about water reliability in a way that metro Perth often forgets, yet the Premier's Statement said nothing about water pressure and quality complaints. He did not talk about ageing pipelines and assets, the cost of keeping small communities supplied, or Water Corporation asset management such as bridges, access roads and load limits stopping traffic in regional Western Australia. He said nothing about that, or the funding needed to fix those ageing assets. Local government has been highlighting water security and ageing infrastructure as a priority issue for years, including reliability and quality. If it is a priority, it actually belongs in the Premier's opening agenda for this year.

When it comes to the environment, announcements without capability will not protect the environment. There was nothing about whether the agencies had the capacity to monitor and enforce, particularly around our threatened ecological communities and compliance issues. The Auditor General's report last year mentioned concerns that many threatened ecological communities are ineffectively monitored and protected, with findings tied back to oversight and conservation performance. There is a system capacity and resourcing problem. This government even refuses to update the state of its environment report. How simple is that? What is the state of the environment? The government does not know and it does not want to know because it will be exposed for its lack of support and funding.

When it comes to energy, people are paying more, businesses are hurting and their Premier's speech did not instil any confidence, I am afraid. The Premier leaned heavily into the transition narrative—batteries, transmission links and renewables as lower cost energy. But that is not the lived reality for many households and businesses right now. Public reporting has highlighted WA businesses facing eye-watering power price increases, with some reporting hikes of 50% or more and raising doubts about transition timing and reliability. Across the market, major energy retailers have been blunt that wholesale price movements may not flow through to households because a growing share of the bill is tied up in poles-and-wire charges, reliability upgrades and the cost of transition infrastructure—costs that do not fall just because wholesale prices do. Western Australians need energy that is affordable and reliable. They are being asked to pay more now, while the system faces major transition risks. Synergy's official price changes page states that the price increases reflect the rising costs to generate and transport electricity, along with the network maintenance and security costs.

heading: Premier's Statement
subject: Premier's Statement
parts: Equally appalling are the health outcomes within the Mid-West area. In the seat of Mid-West, 13% of the population are Aboriginal and 90% of the population live in areas with socio-economic indexes for areas scores in the two quintiles with the highest relative disadvantage and no areas of relative advantage. Potentially preventable hospitalisations are those that could have been prevented through early intervention and disease management, as was outlined in the sustainable health review, often through adequate and accessible primary care. I am drawing this information from a Rural Health West document that covers much of the state of Western Australia. Preventable hospitalisations for Mid-West residents are higher across the three areas of vaccine preventable and acute and chronic illness. These are particularly high in the Murchison area that I represent. We know that chronic conditions are much more prevalent in the population of the Mid-West, especially the Aboriginal population. The six Murchison shires that I represent, including Yalgoo, Mount Magnet, Cue, Meekatharra and Murchison, collectively generate in excess of $3 billion in mineral wealth, according to the Western Australian Mineral and Petroleum Statistics Digest 2023–24. Of course, we know that 18.5 million tonnes of ore that came out of those areas went through the port of Geraldton in 2024–25.

Geraldton's major hospital is an important anchor point for the Mid-West area, but it has issues. We know that the redevelopment project had a very long delay. A couple of years ago when the Auditor General reported on major projects, it was found that that project had been the most delayed of all the major hospital projects. I am very happy to see that finally there will be a hospital there that will better serve the needs of the area. After the work that was done by the member for Geraldton on the campaign, the oncology unit will be delivered at some point in the future. No doubt the member for Geraldton will have further information on that in the future. We know that that is happening only after the government of the day was dragged through a process of public interrogation in that political campaign and elsewhere to get those results.

I spoke a little while ago about Meekatharra Hospital, which was built in 1954. A new one was promised in 2021 by the Premier, but it will not be a new hospital now; it will be just a refurbishment. It is yet to be determined how that will be delivered. I am pleased to see some progress, but the community deserves more clarity about the start, construction timelines et cetera for the hospital build.

heading: State Development Bill 2025
subject: State Development Bill 2025
parts: Members will note that "defence" is the first word in this list.

I turn to compliance and enforcement. Earlier this year, the Office of the Auditor General, which I am sure all members will remember, released two reports. One report related to the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation's capacity to effectively monitor and enforce water licensing conditions. The other reported on the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions' capacity to effectively manage threatened and priority ecological communities. I want to share a small part of what the Office of the Auditor General found in its audits of these two departments. In doing so, I remind members that two of the fundamental requirements of an effective environmental regulatory system are a functioning framework for compliance and enforcement and agencies having the data, information and capacity that they need to monitor and manage key components of the natural environment. Here, the government intends to speed up approvals—we are all in furious agreement about that—and add more projects to the compliance system in the glaring absence of such a framework. In its assessment of the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation, the Office of the Auditor General concluded the following:
DWER does not effectively monitor or enforce the conditions on the more than 12,000 water licences in the State.
This was the assessment of DWER's management of water resources in WA.

In its assessment of the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions' management of threatened ecological communities and priority ecological communities, the Office of the Auditor General concluded that although the department has listed 65 TECs, it is not yet giving full effect to those protections, leaving some more vulnerable than others with legal but not practical protection. The department cannot effectively track nor demonstrate the impact of its practical conservation activities on the condition of TECs. To be protected, TECs need to be formally listed. The department has identified 390 other ecological communities that are threatened, rare, likely threatened or a priority for listing. The report outlines that at its current pace, the department would take over 100 years to list and protect the 390 priority ecological communities if they were all deemed suitable for listing.
The report continues:

The Department has focused its monitoring and protection activities on the 28 per cent of TECs that occur on the land it manages. It has not made significant progress with monitoring the condition of the 72 per cent not on Department-managed land …

heading: State Development Bill 2025
subject: State Development Bill 2025
parts: Hon Stephen Dawson : I am not quite sure I understand the question, but if it is about checks and balances, certainly, a number of checks and balances are included in the bill before us that are sure to uphold the regulatory standards currently in place. These include priority project designation notices and state development area declarations being required to be tabled in Parliament. They are reported on in the Coordinator General's annual report. Modification orders are subject to tabling and disallowance. There are limits on modification order power so they cannot exempt a project from key regulatory authorisations or modify or exclude provisions related to bilateral agreement. There are requirements for the minister to be satisfied that the project will still be effectively regulated before making a modification order. There is the preservation of review rights for decisions made under joint decision notices to ensure robust and accountable decision-making. There are public consultation requirements for the exercise of powers that have a potential broad impact, including when making or amending a state development area plan. There are requirements to consult with affected public authorities before using certain powers to ensure they are used appropriately. heading: Sexual abuse-Government response
subject: Sexual abuse—Government response
parts: That this house expresses grave concern regarding the Western Australian Labor government's continuing unacceptable performance in responding to sexual abuse matters, whether recent or historical and whether involving children or adult survivors.

Today in this motion I will touch on the refusal by the Premier or any minister for almost a full year to be transparent about the failed supervision of an offender alleged to have attacked a woman in her 40s near Whitfords train station on 19 December 2024; allegations from Mr Dion Barber's lawyer that the government regularly fails to act as a model litigant in child abuse matters and the Attorney General's inaction on these concerning allegations; the Premier prioritising the branding of his government and the protection of a minister ahead of responding in a trauma-informed manner to Mr Barber's verdict; the Treasurer's breathtaking ignorance about the contribution of the Insurance Commission of Western Australia in such matters; the Minister for Child Protection's abject failure to ensure that child protection staff ascertain whether a child in care has been a victim of crime during any period they are reported as missing; the Auditor General's damning performance audit report, tabled on 27 November; and my colleague's call for the establishment of an early childhood watchdog.

I rise today to speak on my motion about the government's unacceptable performance in responding to sexual abuse matters, whether recent or historical and whether involving children or adult survivors. This motion is being brought forward at a poignant time in our community during 16 Days in WA. This is a time when we should be united and dedicated to ending violence against women and children. Every survivor has the right to be safe. During this campaign, the government has asked the public to play their part, yet for many years this government has failed to do so itself. First and foremostly, this motion is to ensure that our state protects its children and emphasises the essential qualities of integrity, accountability and transparency. What we speak about today is not politics; it is people. It is who we are and what we stand for, and it shows what happens when there is an imbalance of government power and human vulnerability.

heading: Sexual abuse-Government response
subject: Sexual abuse—Government response
parts: In my mind, one challenge in the current process, in which ECRU sits within the Department of Communities, is that it creates more vulnerability for children in the circumstance that their family has already had interaction with the Department of Communities. It is very difficult for any child who suffers abuse to have their voice heard, and it is even more difficult for a child in a dysfunctional family in which the parents are interacting with the Department of Communities. The child's voice is not being heard; it is filtered through the interaction the department might be having with that family. I have the greatest respect for all those workers. I have a family member who is involved in this sector, and some of the stories that I hear from her are extremely challenging. I commend anyone who has given their life to the child protection sector. It is a very difficult area. I think the structural change that needs to happen is independence, because I think that will remove the conflict of interest between the regulator and the service provider. The problem is that the department will naturally focus on the broader issue. An independent ECRU could really ensure a singular focus on the child. I think that is very important. It would provide more confidence in the community and more transparency and accountability. It aligns with best practice in a regulatory setting. I also think it is important that an independent ECRU would provide a level of advocacy for children and would not worry about what ministerial advisers say to a director general. I have spent a long time in the public service, and I know how large agencies work. This would be a very good reform. I add that idea to my full support of the opposition's position that ECRU needs to be independent and more well resourced. That would be a step forward in the right direction.

I also want to touch on the Auditor General's report. I listened with interest to the minister's response to that report. Hon Nick Goiran correctly stated that the final report was not completed until December 2017. That report highlighted some challenges. It is a very damning report. Everyone in this chamber should avail themselves of that report and go through it. The Auditor General made 400 recommendations. Of those, 310 relate to actions by the Western Australian Government. Many of the recommendations are yet to be implemented. I think the Auditor General said she will continue to focus on them. The report identified the fact that they would continue to examine them. It is almost nine years since the release of that report, and it really highlights that the government should have done better. I think it also highlights the challenges in resourcing and also the fact that we do not seem to be progressing. As far as I can tell from the Auditor General's report, the Northern Territory and Western Australia are the only jurisdictions that have not introduced legislation to address the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations. That is contained in the summary report online. That is a damning indictment on the government given that Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia, partially, have already implemented legislation in relation to that.

I note that Hon Nick Goiran has been very active in this space. Again, we hear these casual kind of answers from the government on this. It is really time to get honest with the people of Western Australia. The government has three years left of its term. It has a real opportunity to do something and leave a legacy for itself in this place if it is not re-elected at the next election. That should not be the reason; it should do this for the good of the community and the benefit of the most vulnerable children. It is an opportunity to leave a legacy.

heading: Sports and Entertainment Trust Bill 2025
subject: Sports and Entertainment Trust Bill 2025
parts: I refer to a modern, skills-based board. Part 3 modernises board governance to ensure the trust is directed by people with the right expertise. The new board will comprise seven members selected for their skills in commerce, law, financial management, human resources, major events, infrastructure management, and sport and public administration. This ensures that strategic, commercial and operational decision-making is informed, expert and aligned with contemporary practice. The bill also introduces clear terms of office, robust conflict-of-interest disclosure requirements, rules for remote meetings and written resolutions, and protections to ensure business continuity. This is governance designed for the next 30 years, not the last.

Stronger accountability to the Parliament and the people is important in any bill. Transparency and accountability are deeply embedded in this bill. Part 4 will empower the minister to issue directions, require the trust to keep the minister informed and ensure full compliance with the Financial Management Act and Auditor General Act. Ministerial access to information is guaranteed. Annual reporting is strengthened. Notices of financial difficulty must be escalated immediately. These mechanisms will ensure that while the trust has commercial flexibility, it remains accountable to Parliament and, ultimately, to the people of Western Australia.

I refer to protecting safety and integrity at our venues. Some of the most important reforms appear in part 5 of the bill. For the first time, we will establish a clear statutory framework for conduct on trust property, replacing reliance on ticket conditions and common law. This includes offences for arena invasion, with penalties of $5,500; powers for trust officers to remove patrons and request personal details; 48-hour bans for noncompliance; a new system of temporary exclusion orders up to five years; and a pathway to permanent exclusion for serious or repeated misconduct. These are important, particularly when managing venues and big events with large numbers of participants and interstate and international guests. This bill also has full rights of review and natural justice via the State Administrative Tribunal. These measures protect players, artists, staff and the tens of thousands of patrons who attend events each week. They will also give the trust tools to maintain safe, inclusive venues without overly relying on police or hirers.

heading: Infrastructure delivery-Government performance
subject: Infrastructure delivery—Government performance
speakerRaw: Ms Libby Mettam (Vasse—Deputy Leader of the Opposition) (4:33 pm)
parts: It was the former Barnett government that delivered one of Western Australia's biggest ever capital works programs, with significant and much-needed infrastructure across the state. Part of that infrastructure was a $7 billion health infrastructure program. This government loves to point the finger at the previous government, and for the moment I will focus on that and what was delivered under the previous government. In respect of the $7 billion of health infrastructure, in the last three years of the Barnett government we saw construction completed on three major metropolitan hospitals—not announcements, but actual delivery. They were Fiona Stanley Hospital, Midland Health Campus and Perth Children's Hospital. We also actually delivered—not just announced—major projects to the regions. Albany Health Campus opened in 2013; Busselton Health Campus was completed in March 2015; Kalgoorlie Hospital was completed in August 2015; and construction commenced on Esperance and Carnarvon health campus redevelopments, to name just a few.

This government looks backwards because of its appalling record over the last nine years. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, there have been no new hospitals under this government's watch; there have been myriad announcements, but nothing delivered. This government likes to look backwards, but what we have actually seen over the last nine years are shocking reports and an appalling record when it comes to what has been delivered on the ground. We saw shocking reports earlier this year regarding the state of Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital, with mould, sewage leaking into intensive care units and ongoing issues with Legionella. The government in 2020 promised an upgrade of the Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital emergency department; that was five years ago. Where is it? Construction is yet to start, some five years after the announcement. The people of Geraldton have been waiting eight years, and counting, for the expansion of Geraldton Health Campus—the most delayed major project, according to a 2023 report by the Auditor General. We also have pity for the people in the health communities of Tom Price, Paraburdoo and Laverton, who have been waiting up to nine years—yes, nine years—for their health infrastructure. We also know that regional residents in communities such as Busselton, Dunsborough, Margaret River and Augusta do not have local access to cancer services and radiation oncology. They have to travel to Bunbury, sometimes daily, for up to six weeks, adding further burden to a trip that is not captured by the Patient Assisted Travel Scheme. That is a booming region of the state, but there is no planning for cancer treatments close to home.

If this government were really serious about a health plan for the future, we would have believed the Premier's talking points in August when he talked about the $50 million health asset maintenance fund, followed by a $500 million major project fund, which was then incorporated into a $1.5 billion health infrastructure fund. That was not announced during the election campaign or during the most recent state budget; it was announced on the back of pressure from the health workers of this state—our nurses and our doctors—the appalling reports coming from our hospitals, and the damning statistics that point to 7,000 hours of ambulance ramping. That is seven times the number that the Premier had referred to as a health crisis. Elective surgery waiting lists are blowing out by over 50%, and children are waiting years—in fact, up to four years—to see a paediatrician.

heading: Infrastructure delivery-Government performance
subject: Infrastructure delivery—Government performance
parts: This Agreement is based on the equivalent of 20% of motor vehicle licence fee collections, being allocated to assist with the improvement and maintenance of the Local Government Road network.

Interestingly, earlier this year, the Office of the Auditor General—Caroline Spencer herself—did a briefing. It did an investigation and audit into where that money was going. As a result of that, it came up with these findings. It found a $205 million disparity between the budgeted vehicle licence fees and the actual fees between 2014 and 2024. According to the report, that could have made $41 million available to local governments based on the 80-20 allocation between state and local government roads. This report shows that money is there and it is time for this state government to assist our local governments. What do we see instead? We see frivolous spending on pet projects here in the Perth metropolitan area, such as racetracks. Like I say, regional MPs drive those roads every single day, as do family members, in either trucks, large vehicles or commuter vehicles. They drive school buses as well. Let me touch on that later in this speech when and if I have time.

I have seen failing road infrastructure across the electorate of Geraldton in particular. Chapman Valley Road is the major arterial road that runs through the heart of the Shire of Chapman Valley. It has been presented to Main Roads through Regional Road Groups in a number of cases. It is a state-owned road, but every other single road within the local government area leads to that major road. That is where all commodities go to the Port of Geraldton. I have to say that it has had no love for the last 12 months. It has a lot of paint markings on it and big circles around big potholes. The pavement is falling apart. The heat itself is causing wheel tracks to form and large mounds of bitumen to come together in the middle of the road, which is actually quite a danger. We know that the number of fatalities on the roads is increasing; it is actually at a record high. It is nothing to be proud of. Yet what do we see? We know the condition of roads is a contributing factor to that. All we and local governments ask, again, is to please listen. They are appointed to the Regional Road Groups. Those Regional Road Groups are there for decision-making. It even states it in this particular document, State Road Funds to Local Government Agreement to Western Australian Local Governments. It outlines why Regional Road Groups are so important. They determine policymaking and improvements needed in Western Australia's road network. They mean state road funds to local governments can have a local decision-making contribution and a priority list for the state government to consider, yet what do we see? We see a failing road system across Western Australia. I have talked to truckers and I have spoken with Heather Jones. She is very well known across the trucking landscape. She runs Pilbara Heavy Haulage Girls Group and sits on a national representative body. I recently caught up with her and she said to me that the state of the roads is absolutely appalling. She does thousands of thousands of kilometres across Western Australia and sometimes across the Nullarbor. The interconnecting freight networks underpin our retailers and our industries and what it would mean to run the state of Western Australia. She says that truck stops within Western Australia are poorly maintained or non-existent and I would have to agree.

heading: Infrastructure delivery-Government performance
subject: Infrastructure delivery—Government performance
parts: As of late 2025, connection times have increased 180% since 2020. Small residential connections are taking 12 months or more. Serviced land is running short while population and construction demand continues to rise. This is not just a market cycle; it is a system that has been under-maintained. The people who are hurting are the teachers, nurses and police, particularly in regional Western Australia, who cannot find a home. Our businesses are being held back. They cannot expand because they cannot get the workers living in the towns where they need them. We do not want more announcements. We do not want more promises. Western Australians do not want to hear more promises and announcements. They want the land, they want the housing and they want the approvals and infrastructure they need to live.

We know that the public housing system is failing and its maintenance is in a terrible situation. The Auditor General report was damning. Maintenance costs have risen 44% since 2019, but the actual maintenance activity is up only 7%. Eighty-five per cent of maintenance is reactive instead of planned, so that is more expensive. The department has spent $256 million on travel and overheads since 2019. We see that constant work order changes have added another $162 million and only 51% of vacant property maintenance is completed within the targeted time. This is fundamental infrastructure for affordable and social housing and GROH housing in our regions. The result is predictable. Thousands of families wait for housing while properties sit empty for weeks or months because the system is bloated and poorly managed. Spending more money is not the same as delivering better outcomes. People do not need promises, they need delivery. Western Australians can tell the difference.

I would like to complete my contribution by talking more specifically about my local region, particularly around Murray–Wellington. Regional WA knows that talk and delivery are two different things. Nowhere is the failure more obvious than in the regions where people feel the gap between promises and real outcomes every single day. I will give members some examples. I have not spoken about the Pinjarra Heavy Haulage Deviation for a while. I thought I would bring it back into discussion here. It has been talked about since the 1990s. It has been planned since the 1990s, and in 2017, 85% of the local town site went to a referendum asking for it to be delivered. We have 800 trucks a day going through the main street of town and they are dangerous trucks. They shut down the whole town. We have two schools on that main street and I have watched the kids running around these huge trucks when they get stuck at the traffic lights going through the town. We have been promised a heavy haulage deviation for years. We had the money; it was taken away by the federal government.
