heading: State Development Bill 2025
subject: State Development Bill 2025
parts: We need to re-democratise our decision-making. We need to explore other approaches like blockchain for getting the opinion of the people and citizen councils. We need to re-centralise decision-making in a small executive circle. We just now in WA, in this chamber, are at a fork in the road. One path leads to more participatory, transparent and technologically enabled democracy; the other leads to a highly centralised discretionary executive who can rewrite the rules for each favoured project. The choice is ours.

As a GP, I am required to obtain informed consent, disclose the risks and act with prudence. I am accountable to independent professional bodies. This bill does not require informed community consent. It downplays long-term health and environmental risks and lacks robust independent oversight. It lacks mandatory engagement with the Environmental Protection Authority. It lacks mandatory engagement with the Auditor General on the integrity body for each use of modification orders. If doctors practised the way this bill proposes to govern—hiding information, rushing decisions and moving goal posts—we would lose our licences. I put forward that we need to think more of a service to the many, not favours for the few. Even if they might offer a job to a member retiring from Parliament to work for one of the major companies or offer to give a large donation to the member's party if they do something for them, let us serve the people, not the few. Let us get the truth. Let us get some transparency in here about the real trade-offs of development because no-one doubts that we need to have a streamlined approach to opening up our state to proper development. We need that. We must have that because we are actually helping to fund the rest of our great nation. We need this, but this bill is not it. We need long-term wellbeing. We do not need short electoral cycle choices.

In short, this is not a bill I can support in any shape or form. It is not a legislative expression of service and truth; it is an expression of speed and secrecy. What are the alternatives? I am going to suggest that we pause this bill. I am going to stand against it. I am going to ask for it to be sent to the Standing Committee on Legislation if members are going to take it forward. It is not right that we put this bill onto our people. They trust us to do the right thing. They trust us to serve them. They trust us to put legislation forward that serves the people first and foremost. We need the transnationals for that business we have here—we must have that—but we are not serving the people with this bill. We are serving the transnationals first and foremost.

This problem has been going on for a long time. I remember when I lived in Willagee 10 years ago, a Homeswest property was opposite where I lived. It was demolished, and the land stood there for three years doing nothing. When I wrote to the minister at the time—I think it was Hon Troy Buswell—I was told that it was all about rezoning and it would be solved, but it took such a long time. We need to make this sort of issue a priority.

One Nation has always been on the front foot on this issue. Immigration is an issue. That does not mean that I demonise migrants. If we cannot have that conversation, it is a very sad state of affairs. I refer to one of Hon Colin Tincknell's speeches in 2018 when he warned of a looming housing crisis and here we are years later and it is upon us. Once again, One Nation was the voice in the wilderness speaking the truth and now Australians are waking up and catching up, and will be coming over to our party.

heading: Government Regional Officers' Housing-Government performance
subject: Government Regional Officers' Housing—Government performance
parts: It is the same for police. Police want to keep our communities safe. Our child protection workers do the same. They do the hardest jobs, yet we cannot find them a house. These are public servants who are trying to do the right thing and we are letting them down.

We are talking about Government Regional Officers' Housing. We all know it as GROH. It is a critically important program. We know it is the backbone of essential services in regional Western Australia. Without GROH, as I have said, many communities simply cannot function properly. Despite its importance, we know that the program is under severe strain. I would like to take an honest look at the situation. We see the same picture in Hansard, the Auditor General's recent reports and the Department of Communities and the Department of Housing and Works' own reports, and we hear in the words of frontline workers—we heard some of their words and some of their situations described today by the member for Central Wheatbelt—that this program is no longer meeting the needs of the state, no longer meeting its purpose and no longer meeting the expectations of the communities it is meant to support. It is just no longer meeting the needs it was designed for.

This is the current state of GROH. According to government figures, the GROH portfolio currently includes around 5,519 properties at any one time, although currently about 612 are vacant. That means that one of every nine GROH homes is currently empty. Regional schools are struggling to attract teachers, as I have said, our hospitals are short staffed and our police stations cannot fill vacancies. I spoke to a police sergeant down in my electorate who had to wait months and months before they could actually take the job because they just could not find a house. It puts a lot of pressure on the existing staff, the individual and their families. We know that turnover happens in around a third of GROH tenancies each year. We know that is true. Even accounting for turnover, which we know is understandable, vacancy rates that high, with hundreds of homes sitting empty, show us that the system is not really in balance. I am sure we can do better. It is a system that is not in balance and tells of delays in maintenance, delays in allocation and delays in basic administration. I know the people who administer these programs and I am sure they are working hard, but the systems, the tools, they have are letting them down. The computer systems and the monitoring are letting them down. That tells us of a system struggling to do its basic job in putting a roof over the head of essential workers, which is what we are talking about here.

I think the minister understands these issues and is acting in good faith. I will give him that. I believe he is acting in good faith and is working hard. He is a hardworking minister, but the system and the hand he has been dealt is difficult. The funding he has been allowed to execute in this situation is only now starting to trickle through. Look, I really feel for the minister. I am sure there are many competing issues and he has to work hard to get the funding, but Government Regional Officers' Housing is an area that really needs focus. I encourage the minister to make sure that he is fighting harder for those most affected workers.

Let us talk about the Auditor General's report on the maintenance system for a moment. The maintenance system is in disarray. We know that market pressures are only part of the story. The Auditor General's report this year found that the government does not even know the condition of most of its regional housing stock, which, of course, includes GROH houses. The report said that only 19% of properties have an up-to-date condition assessment. No wonder people are moving in and finding things broken and locks not fixed. They do not know. The system does not even tell them. Only 19% of those properties have a full condition report. That means that four in five homes lacked that basic condition data.

This is the 21st century. Surely we can have an asset report that tells us the state of the government's own properties—the regional houses. It should not be that hard. Of maintenance, 85% is now reactive. We know that reactive maintenance is the most expensive type of maintenance a house can have. If someone has to call someone out urgently, they are going to jack up the prices. Under the contract, they are allowed to do that. They are obviously not doing preventive or predictive maintenance. They are having to do reactive maintenance, and that is not acceptable in the 21st century. It is not acceptable for anyone—certainly not in Western Australia.

That means that maintenance costs have risen by 44% from $213 million to over $300 million since 2019, but actual maintenance activity has only increased by 7%. The cost has gone up but the activity has only increased by 7%. Apart from that, travel costs alone have hit $256 million. It is a quarter of a billion dollars over six years for travel, including $75 million on non-urgent jobs that should have been bundled together. On average, there are 1.1 variations per job, costing $162 million. That is $162 million in variations. The first thing builders look for is a variation. A builder has to make sure they get a few variations in there because that is how they make their money. They attend the job, cut it to the bone and then get them on the variations. This government has been got on the variations, which have cost this government $162 million according to the Auditor General. Only 5.7% of jobs are audited.
(Member's time extended.)

Mr David Bolt : Of those, one third showed noncompliance. The department recovers about $1 million a year, but the Auditor General estimates that the real amount of overcharging could exceed $12 million annually. If we combine that with 612 vacant homes sitting idle, we have a system that is failing at both ends: before tenants move in and while they are living there looking for maintenance jobs to be provided for them on time.

Why does this matter? This is not only about housing. It is about workforce stability, economic resilience and, of course, the ultimate viability of our regional towns. When our teachers cannot get housing, schools are affected. When nurses cannot get housing, emergency departments go understaffed. When police cannot get housing, public safety suffers. When child protection workers cannot get housing, vulnerable children who need it most go without care. A housed workforce is the foundation of every regional community and they deserve better than what they are getting.

heading: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
subject: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
parts: When I provided my previous grievance to the Minister for Local Government, it was uppermost in my mind that the community was affected by the significant amount of debt that the Shire of Coolgardie had got itself into. Figures being publicly discussed are up towards $30 million worth of debt, so who is this debt going to affect? Is it the member for Geraldton? No. It is going to affect the hardworking ratepayers in my community. It is their services and projects that will be affected. I have met with so many community members who are outraged about how the shire had managed to get itself into so much debt and how it is going to get out of it.

For the Hansard record, I wish to reiterate that the minister and I have met with the Shire of Coolgardie many times to discuss its position, plans, any boundary adjustments and general concerns, in addition to those discussions about its request to adjust its rates massively. I would be delighted to meet with the member for Geraldton to put her right on the numbers of meetings that have been held and who was there so that she has more than one source of information about the facts. I was in constant contact with the minister as she waded through all the information relating to Coolgardie, because the information and facts are very important to my ratepayers, unlike members opposite. During this time, the Liberal Party ran a public session to create significant division and uncertainty amongst community members. To what end? Of course, we know that the minister held a community forum at which she provided a 12-month breather to allow the shire to get its finances in order. Let us be clear; as the minister said at the time, in the history of local government in this state, no council has ever had a debt of the scale that the Shire of Coolgardie has. I hope that the debt can be significantly reduced, and I welcome the minister's tough approach on what the shire needs to now report on every quarter. If this is onerous on the shire, so be it. It is what the community expects and what I am looking forward to. It is a shame that the member for Geraldton feels that this is too much for the shire to provide. I ask the member whether she has read the report of the Office of the Auditor General. It cited shocking mismanagement and poor governance as causes of the financial situation. It also said that there was a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt about the ability of the shire to continue as a going concern. Key findings included a significant loss for the year ending 30 June 2024, when liabilities exceeded assets by more than $14.2 million, plus improper dismissals at that time.

At the end of the day, there was a situation and there were only so many options available for Coolgardie. People said to me that Coolgardie could spend all its dollars servicing the debt so that the community suffers, as it already has, with savings measures that see fewer services and community buildings and activities, or Coolgardie could spend money servicing the community and then keep, for want of a better term, trading insolvent. Either outcome is unsustainable. There has been substantial commentary and discussion about the Shire of Coolgardie's financial performance, which has understandably caused a lot of concern within the community. During this time, a huge amount of misinformation has been circulated. I hear it every day.

heading: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
subject: Local Government Amendment (Rating of Certain Mining Licences) Bill 2025
parts: When I was in Kalgoorlie with my good friend Hon Julie Freeman a number of weeks ago, we took the opportunity to meet with the local government of the City of Kalgoorlie–Boulder and talk about this issue. I was born in Kalgoorlie. I have a long history with the town, with my grandfather being the CEO of the Chamber of Commerce for over two decades. He started the regional Chamber of Commerce in Western Australia. So I know the people of Kalgoorlie well—and Coolgardie, because we have to drive through Coolgardie if we are travelling from my electorate into the greater Goldfields region. When we spoke to people from the Shire of Coolgardie, we knew how the meeting went with the minister at the time and that people felt deeply aggrieved with the way that they were treated with that process. That was a matter of the public record and was reported in the media.

It just goes to show that if the government of Western Australia and the Minister for Local Government were willing to sweep away a local government like Coolgardie for political purposes and then blame a dodgy former CEO, then regional Western Australia should be very careful of this minister and this government because they have form. To the 28 local governments in my electorate of Central Wheatbelt, I say: watch this minister and this government very carefully when it comes to the demonising of local councils. They have put in ridiculous guardrails around some of our regional local governments, basically overregulating them out of operation. Many councils in the electorate of Central Wheatbelt face things like local government audit fees. I know that 8% of the Shire of Beverley's budget goes to the Auditor General for audit fees. This is just a ridiculous amount when it has an annual budget of probably eight million bucks.

This government clearly has an issue with local government. We heard Western Australian Local Government Association president Karen Chappel's damning assessment of a senior frontbencher of this government. Does the minister agree with Karen Chappel's assessment of Minister Carey and the way he is treating local governments in this state? I put on notice the way that this government is behaving towards regional local governments. heading: Health-Gender Diversity Service Model of Care-Minors
subject: Health—Gender Diversity Service Model of Care—Minors
parts: The government is hiding behind the veil of cabinet-in-confidence. It goes out into the community and makes up stories. We saw the government's lies on the amount of money that would be saved from this. We saw the Wyllie Group say that that was completely wrong. Something in the order of $36 million, from recollection, had been allocated for it in the budget, so the savings in the budget were virtually minimal. There were no savings. I think half of that, or most of that, has already been spent on a business case. Remember, folks, this is our money; it is the money of the people of Western Australia. That issue was pushed aside because it suited the government's narrative on the day to say that it was ending the convention centre project and was saving all that money that would be put into health. It was trying to get around the narrative that has become clear in the minds of the community that this government has its priorities wrong. The government is trying to rebut it using a very unfashionable statement in relation to the savings. We have asked for the business case but were told it is cabinet-in-confidence. Not only that, it cannot even be explained. We do not even get half-truths about what is going on with the PCEC.

People here might say that it is just Hon Neil Thomson saying all those things and the opposition and the crossbench are all grizzling about the lack of transparency and they do not deserve to have that information. What does the Auditor General say? Let us have a look at what the Auditor General says about some of these things. I think it is unprecedented in the history of Western Australia that we have an Auditor General who has to, on an ongoing basis, raise with the community the lack of transparency of this government. There have to be some learnings here for the government. It has another three years of its term to run. I do not think it will be re-elected in 2029 because I think people are tired of it. I talk to people out there, and people are really tired of the way they have been treated. We see appalling behaviour from some ministers, particularly the Minister for Planning and Lands in the way he is treating the local government sector to the point that there has been an unprecedented response from the Western Australian Local Government Association. It came out to say, "This is not on. We're tired of the abuse that's being poured upon us constantly and of being used, effectively, as the whipping boy in relation to any failure of this government." The government is not taking any responsibility.

Let us have a look at what the Auditor General said on 15 August. The Auditor General, Caroline Spencer, said that the government had denied her office access to information relating to Griffin Coal's insolvency. I mean, how bad is that? This is the Auditor General; it is not just us—the terrible Liberal Party that wants to weaponise everything. Those are not my words; I am just saying that that is the attitude we get. Maybe it is the Australian Christians wanting to grab a few things to get a few headlines, or maybe it is the Greens wanting to run a few stories in relation to the government's lack of action on the climate or the environment. That is the attitude of this government—dismissive of everything other than its own party machine—but this is actually the Auditor General who is complaining. Surely that should encourage a moment of reflection by this government, and for it to actually say, "Hang on a minute. This is a serious issue. We should probably be a bit more forthcoming about it."
I like the wording of the second paragraph of this motion:
Expresses concern that the documents were only provided after numerous requests in Parliament were denied, and after notice of motion was given to compel the production of this document.

The government is going to be forced into it, because we were going to make it do it. There was a level of frustration across the crossbench and the opposition bench to force the government to do this. Suddenly, we have a level of cooperation but, unfortunately, the Auditor General had already said that this information had not been provided. Of course, after the Auditor General spoke to the media, the government disclosed the amount in Parliament, so we finally got an answer. It is the same pattern; it is exactly the same pattern.

I imagine the Auditor General is not somebody who would want to just get up and go to the media as the first port of call when she does not receive documents. I imagine the Auditor General would first write to the minister and ask for that information. There would then be a letter back. The Auditor General would be a little frustrated and someone from the office would get on the phone to the chief of staff. There would be some communication going on: "Come on. Surely you can provide this information. It's vital for my review." I am sure there would have been several iterations of that request communicated back and forth. Being the very good, excellent public servant that she is, the Auditor General would not want to just go out there and make a big scene about this, but she had to get to the point at which she could finally come out and speak about the legal fees that were part of the Griffin Coal insolvency. That, to me, demonstrates a huge amount of frustration, which members probably heard in the voice of Hon Maryka Groenewald—this finally happened only after being pushed by the Auditor General. The honourable member is in good company—the company of the Auditor General; she is not the only one.

Let us look at some of the other things the Auditor General has said. I have read about transparency issues several times in reports from the Auditor General. This media statement from 16 June 2025 is headed "Transparency needed on State's major IT projects to give the Parliament and community an accurate picture on project progress and costs". That seems like a really sensible thing to do. Again, the Auditor General has had to put out a media release like this. That is damning for the government. If it happened only once or twice, maybe the government could say, "Oh well, someone miscommunicated and we just didn't get our act together", but when we start getting that over and over again, we know it is becoming a major problem.
I will quote some comments in this media release of 16 June. The Auditor General is quoted as stating:
We found publicly available information on IT projects is patchy, inconsistent and not transparent.

It is the same message again. Members on this side do not have to be Einstein to find evidence of this government's lack of transparency; we just have to go online and look up the phrase "lack of transparency" and see what we get. We get a pile of it, and we are getting more and more, especially from the Auditor General. The media release continues:
The estimated total cost of the 10 projects we reviewed is at least $1.6 billion more than the $2.6 billion initially advised to Government by entities, with further increases expected.

This is not small change; we are not talking about small change here. We are talking about large amounts of money—a billion-dollar black hole in the budget. There are a billion dollars worth of projects that were not even provided to the Auditor General. This is a major, major problem, and I think in the history of Western Australia in time to come—no doubt, after this government changes—we are going to see this whole issue exposed. Governments fall down through a lack of transparency and the sort of arrogance that shows through in this government's defensive attitude. Hon John Carey is one example of the government's extremely defensive behaviour, particularly in the planning space. We see that behaviour in his constant attacks and deflections. We also see the defensive behaviour of the Treasurer, Hon Rita Saffioti, in relation to some of the other big projects that I am going to mention now. We know about Hon Rita Saffioti's vanity projects. I have at times implored the backbench of the Labor Party to stand up to Hon Rita Saffioti and to take her on in caucus. I encourage members of the backbench of the Labor Party to do that; it is time to step up. If they want to keep their jobs in 2029, now is their chance. I should not be giving them advice on how to do better at the next election, but now is their chance. We have seen Hon Rita Saffioti constantly making captain's calls on projects like the racetrack at Burswood. The expenditure there is allegedly $216 million, but we know that it is not going to be $216 million; it is probably going to be $500 million, because we know the pattern of spending of this profligate Treasurer who has consistently, over time, not kept to her budget.

We saw that with the NRL project but only after a huge amount of work by the Leader of the Opposition, Basil Zempilas, calling for the release of economic modelling in relation to the C-series rail project and the $65 million of taxpayers' money that has been spent on a sports club through deals done over the phone. I am sure someone thought it was a good idea. We see projects suddenly coming to fruition at the stroke of a pen, without the proper work having been done; or, if there has been work done, the economic modelling has not been released to the community to make an assessment. These are the sorts of challenges that this opposition will not resile from. We will stand up to the government, and I know the crossbench supports us on this, because we have to bring transparency back into the Parliament of Western Australia. We have to bring back more openness and honesty to how things are done, and when things do not work properly they should be scrutinised, because that is the only way that we can improve. That is the only way we can get the right treatment for people in our hospitals and it is the only way we can get better economic outcomes in this state. It is the only way we can ensure that we do not see the enormous waste that we are seeing with this government, which seems to have an open chequebook for Hon Rita Saffioti to sign off on these projects. That is what has to change.

subject: Health—Gender Diversity Service Model of Care—Minors
parts: Ministers have issued section 82 notices in Parliament 39 times since coming to power, compared with 55 times during Colin Barnett's second term as premier and just 12 in his first term.

parts: Let me thank members of the opposition and my colleagues on the crossbench for their contributions and for sharing some of the problems they have experienced. parts: 1016. Hon Steve Martin to the parliamentary secretary representing the Minister for Transport:

I refer to the 2009 and 2016 Auditor General's reports into the Main Roads Western Australia maintenance backlog, which both quote figures of approximately $800 million, and the minister's response to my question without notice 985 on 11 November 2025 asking for an updated figure, which was to provide a $22 million figure for year-on-year carryover. Using the Auditor General's definition for the backlog, in dollar terms what is the most recently assessed figure for the Main Roads' maintenance backlog and approximately how many kilometres of road are included in this figure?
Hon Samantha Rowe replied:
I thank the honourable member for some notice of the question and provide the following answer on behalf of the Minister for Transport.
